speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE IN FIGHTING FOREST FIRES-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43.
Since the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broad-bent) has been quoted in the press as having confused Manitoba officials by stating that the provinces are liable for 100 per cent of the costs of military aid in firefighting, and considering that provinces are not charged for salaries of regular armed forces members employed in firefighting-nor are they charged for use and maintenance of equipment-and considering that charges made to the provinces for incremental costs are, in fact, a small percentage of the costs of the Department of National Defence to provide these services, and that this represents a much smaller cost to the provinces than such services provided by other sources, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke (Mr. Hopkins):
That the Leader of the New Democratic Party correct his statement regarding services supplied by the armed forces in order to eliminate the confusion he has caused and in order to give credit to the very excellent work of the Canadian Armed Forces in assisting the provinces and Canadian citizens threatened by forest fires.

subsubtopic: CONVENING OF JUSTICE AND LEGAL AFFAIRS COMMITTEE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
The Thirty-second Parliament has now been in session for some 44 days, and as yet there has been absolutely no move to

May 28, 1980
organize the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. In view of the fact that there are important questions of immediate national urgency facing our country, involving the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General, among others, and there has been no action by the government to constitute this important committee, I have made arrangements, in connection with the appropriate House officials, for a committee room and time to assemble interested members of Parliament to constitute and organize this committee. Therefore, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence):
That this House directs that the organizational meeting of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs be held at 8 p.m. on Thursday, the 29th day of May, 1980, at room 306, West Block.

subsubtopic: DAMAGE CAUSED BY FOREST FIRES-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that forest fires are raging throughout parts of several provinces, especially Ontario, Quebec and the prairies, and that some of these are still out of control, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm):
That the Minister of the Environment conduct immediately an assessment of the damages inflicted by those fires on Canada's over-all environment, including Canada's inventory of accessible forest stocks, and that he table the results of such an assessment without any delay.

subsubtopic: REQUEST CRIMINAL CODE BE AMENDED TO CONFORM WITH BILL OF RIGHTS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, under Standing Order 43, to present an urgent and pressing matter.
Whereas the Canadian Bill of Rights guarantees the rights of individuals to life, and whereas an unborn child is an
individual, and whereas thousands of unborn individuals are denied the right to life because of our abortion laws, I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper):
That this House urge the government to bring in legislation to amend the Criminal Code in regard to abortions, to conform with the Canadian Bill of Rights.

subsubtopic: DEMONSTRATION ON PARLIAMENT HILL-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
Whereas the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) did not appear in front of the Parliament buildings today to receive the presentation of the public employees of this country in their protest of the meagre 5 per cent raise they have been offered, as opposed to the first-class air travel offered to members of Parliament, which they do not want, the 7 per cent raise that is given in the first year to members of Parliament, and the fact that we had a 9.1 per cent increase in the cost of living last year, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy):
That this House suspend its regular duties momentarily to have the House accept the presentation in the form of a wooden nickel that we would like to present at this time to the President of the Treasury Board.

subsubtopic: STUDENT PARTICIPATION IN CAUSE OF NATIONAL UNITY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the fact Quebec's referendum resulted in strong support for Canadian unity, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga):
That this House acknowledge the message received from the students of the history club of Notre Dame College, in Wilcox, Saskatchewan, who are deeply conscious of the strong attachment of the French Canadians of the province of Quebec to their culture and their determination to work for a renewed federal-
May 28, 1980

ism. I would like to pledge their good will to work toward understanding the Quebec viewpoint and thus facilitate a frank dialogue toward a more prosperous, equitable and serene federalism which will result in a stronger Canada.

subsubtopic: FUTURE OF POST OFFICE IN FREETOWN, P.E.I.-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that there is widespread fear among the residents of Freetown, P.E.I., that the Freetown post office may be closed, and in view of the fact that almost 100 per cent of the boxholders using that post office have signed a petition against the closing, which has been sent to the Postmaster General, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. McMillan):
That this House instruct the Postmaster General to immediately make known to this House, as well as the residents of Freetown, his plans for the Freetown post office, so that he can honour his commitment made in this House on April 17, 1980, that being that he would consult with the elected representatives of the Parliament before any reductions in postal service would be made.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is to the Prime Minister, who I am sure shares my satisfaction at the positive attitude taken by governments across the country to the prospect of co-operating to reform the constitution. The Prime Minister knows the importance of nurturing that good will if we are, in fact, to achieve that kind of reform.
Oral Questions
My question concerns the action of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who yesterday, in a prepared speech, suggested that the motives of the government of Alberta were " to get economic sovereignty with political association".
1 wonder if the Prime Minister would tell the House whether the Minister of Energy was speaking for the federal government when he attributed a motive of sovereignty-association to the government of Alberta?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: What did you say, Marc?

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I agree with the Leader of the Opposition that we must maintain the spirit of Canadianism which has emerged in the past weeks. I have to admit that I have not read the speech that he refers to, although it is my custom to attempt to do so in advance. I have not had the occasion to do so at this time. However, I am informed by the minister that he mentioned no province in his speech.

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Watch your nose, Pinocchio.

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, let me direct a question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. He will recall, having read the speech last night-a deliberately prepared speech-that the great bulk of the references prior to that particular paragraph were to the province of Alberta. If the minister was not referring to the province of Alberta, will he stand in his place and assure the House that he does not accuse that government of those motives; and will he tell the House of Commons to whom he was referring?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I must point out that the Leader of the Opposition, in his question, misquoted what I said by saying it applied to the government of Alberta. The paragraph in question reads as follows:
We just came out of a referendum in which we fought hard for a united Canada. We defeated those who wanted political sovereignty with economic association. We did not carry out this difficult battle to get economic sovereignty with political association.
That is the end of the paragraph.

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: That is the sum total of the paragraph, Madam Speaker, and if the Leader of the Opposition thinks that the hat fits the government of Alberta, that is his judgment.

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Energy, whose reputation and capacity for reconciliation is unparalleled in the land, will know that the immediately preceding seven, eight or nine paragraphs in that speech referred specifically to the province of Alberta. The conclusion was there to be drawn,

May 28, 1980
Oral Questions
and has been drawn by commentators and no doubt by the government of Alberta.
But the minister can clear it up. He can stand in his place now and make a categorical statement that he does not accuse the government of Alberta of those motives, and he can tell us to whom he did direct those comments, to whom he was referring when he made that statement from a prepared text yesterday.

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition referred to the immediately preceding paragraph.

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Try honesty.

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Tell the truth.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
Calm down:
Economically, looking ahead, Canadians have every reason for optimism.

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Answer the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
We have barely begun to tap oil and gas in our Arctic and offshore territories. If we can survive politically, we can, in not too many years, be the strongest democracy in the world. And we can survive if we realize that our fortune and our freedoms hinge on our interdependence.
That is the preceding paragraph.

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
The following paragraph, which 1 quoted in this House just now, applies to any and all provincial governments to whom it may fit. It applies also to the whole of our country.
As I said, we fought hard in the province of Quebec in particular to ensure that the solutions to the problems in this country would be within the federal system. I think we should fight just as hard against all those who are going around and saying that the federal government-

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Who?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Order, please. I will now allow the minister to complete his answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: I will finish by saying that the hat fits so many people on the other side, I will let them pass judgment.

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will spare the House the tedium of reading earlier paragraphs, except perhaps initial sentences in them, those immediately preceding the ones cited by the minister.
The first one, "The Alberta government"; the next one, "The Alberta government"; next "But in fact, Alberta's conventional oil revenues"; and, "Alberta's industrial base." They
are clear references to one province. Now the Minister of Energy has broadened his accusations not simply to deal with the province of Alberta to which he was referring in the prelude of this statement but to include members on this side of the House of Commons.
Will he tell the House of Commons who, specifically, he had in mind? Who is this enemy that he wants to have the Government of Canada take on? Who is the straw man? With whom is he seeking a conflict and a war as we enter a period that is designed to achieve agreement on constitutional reform? Who are the enemies here, in the minds of the Government of Canada?

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: The answer is very simple, Madam Speaker. Indeed, it applies to all those in this country, whoever they are, who think that this country can still go on as a federal country while turning the federal government into a mere agency of the provinces. We do not believe that this is the way of the future of this country.

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. In the interests of calm, I want to point out to him that that paragraph-

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Question.

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Really, Madam Speaker, 1 think this is a terribly crucial thing leading up to the June 9 conference. The minister will realize that if it is not Alberta, then Saskatchewan, British Columbia and Newfoundland could all interpret that speech, with every justification, as referring to them. If the minister does not intend that, surely in the interests of this forthcoming conference he will wish to take this opportunity to correct what one might suggest is a wrong assumption. I give him that opportunity at this moment. If he was not directing his remarks to Alberta, will he clarify that neither is he directing them to those other three provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am not going to add anything to what I said.

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: It is quite clear in my speech. I specifically said in my speech earlier that as far as the producing provinces are concerned, their viewpoint is understandable. The government of Alberta has argued it well and forcefully. What is not so well understood is the federal viewpoint. What I have stated is the perception of Canada as I see it and as I believe this side of the House sees it. That is what we are going to defend.

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
My supplementary question is to the Prime Minister, who not many days ago led this House in one of the

May 28, 1980

most moving afternoons that we have ever spent, in my view. I give him full marks for it. But I am terribly distressed when I see the reaction of various provinces, particularly Alberta, because for some reason they thought those remarks were directed right at them, though I am equally concerned with the other provinces I have mentioned.
So would the Prime Minister please take this opportunity to indicate that the minister was maybe negotiating, by long distance, a new energy contract or something like that, and that it had nothing to do with constitutional discussion? In the interest of all of us, not in a partisan interest, would he please take this opportunity to correct what is obviously a very bad proposition advanced by his colleague?

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: I accept the plea put forward by the hon. member, and I want to tell him that as far as the government is concerned we will approach the meeting which has now been arranged for June 9 in the conciliatory spirit which was present in this House last week. But I would add, because of the previous questions and the debate which has taken place, that the minister was not speaking in a vacuum. We have heard premiers take some pretty strong positions.

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Who?

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Name them.

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: I do not think members opposite are ignorant of what several premiers have defined in the past few weeks.

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Which ones?

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on the one hand I have a member who is asking me to be conciliatory, and on the other I have the Leader of the Opposition who is asking me to name names. I will name one name for starters, and I apologize in advance to the premier for bringing him into the debate.
Premier Peckford was here on the evening the referendum votes were counted, and he defined federalism, the federal government, as an agency of the provinces. Now, this is not our view. I hope it is not the view of the opposition. I am not sure if it is the view of Mr. Peckford himself; perhaps it is a bargaining position. I am prepared to receive him with open arms in spite of his statement but I think he should realize that there are people on this side who do not accept his image of the federal government as being a mere agent of the provinces. That is what the minister is staking out as our position, and in that I support him.

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
A final supplementary. I can agree with the concern about Premier Peckford's speech with respect to the federal government being an agency, though I respect his right to say it. What concerns me is that the Prime Minister now seems to be associating himself with the sovereignty-associa-
Oral Questions
tion implications in the address given by the Minister of Energy last night. 1 hope I have misinterpreted him, but that was the nature of the Prime Minister's answer to me. The talk about the federal government being an agency is not sovereignty-association.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Order, please. It must be a question, not argumentation about what has just been heard. Please ask a very brief question, because the hon. member is on his third question.

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Without wishing to embarrass his colleague, will the Prime Minister make it clear that he dissociates himself from any idea of accusing any premier, of whatever province, of advocating sovereignty-association?

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Obviously not, because there was a referendum battle fought in Quebec precisely on that issue. But if the hon. member is talking about accusing any province of seeking economic sovereignty in political union, I think there have been signs in Canada of a tendency to downgrade the federal government and to give the provinces a type of overwhelming economic "say", which would be corrosive to the type of Canada we seek. I believe there are a lot of people in Canada who share this worry and who would only applaud-

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Do you?

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Yes, I applaud the dichotomy made by the minister, in the sense that there can be dangerous tendencies not only toward political sovereignty of provinces but toward economic sovereignty of provinces, and I support him.

subsubtopic: ALBERTA-COMMENT OF MINISTER OF ENERGY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: DEMONSTRATION ON PARLIAMENT HILL BY MEMBERS OF PSAC-NEGOTIATIONS TO SETTLE DISPUTE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is to the President of the Treasury Board. Visitors to the Hill today from the Public Service Alliance of Canada were disappointed that the minister did not come out to receive a rather large token of their small esteem. By the way, that token is in my office and the minister can pick it up after the question period.
In view of the fact that the clerical and regulatory group of the PSAC have been without a contract since last November, and in view of the rather successful intervention of the Postmaster General in the postal workers' dispute, would the President of the Treasury Board please intervene personally in the negotiations which are going on with the clerical component, and make sure that the offer is more than the paltry 5 per cent being offered at the present time?

May 28, 1980
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, last night I started to speak on this bill and I have a few preliminary comments. I wanted to assure hon. gentlemen opposite that we have no intention of rushing this bill to authorize a $12 billion borrowing authority by the government through this House. We are going to be just as quick in rushing this bill through as the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) becomes quick in answering questions about the economic and financial shape of this country.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: He is not even here.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
If we go by his example since April 14, he is in slow motion. He is stuck in the bog. He is stuck in the tar sands somewhere because he has not answered a question yet.
Why are we not going to rush this bill through? It is because in his speech last night the minister gave us no information. He said that on April 1, 1980 he had $2.9 billion in borrowing authority left, but he did not deign to tell this House how much of the $2.9 billion is left today.
The minister is forgetting that I have a little black book- the book that was prepared for me when I brought in the borrowing authority bill last October 23. It contained all the information current to that date. I know that the minister has a little black book but he is not sharing the content of it with us. He wants to keep it secret. We have some questions which I am going to put on the record in a few minutes.
The Minister of Finance claims to be the genius who arranged for the defeat of our government on the non-confidence motion on December 13 on the budget that we brought down.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
The party that brought down our government on our budget which outlined the way we saw the economy needed to be handled for the next several years. Surely having done that, they accepted the responsibility to bring in their own budget outlining their own approach to the economic and financial problems of Canada as soon as they had the chance. They have been in power now 86 long days. It is like a sentence of 86 years. They have been in office since March 3 and not one new initiative in the economic or financial area have they taken.
The minister does not want to tell us about the budget or that he is going to bring down a budget. I will illustrate how he answers questions in just a moment.
The kind of thing that we and the people of Canada want to know was asked the other day in an article in The Globe and Mail written by Wayne Cheveldayoff, a very astute financial reporter. I have liked him very much since last January 1-in particular since then. I will quote from this article of May 26 as follows:
The big policy question in Ottawa these days is what, if anything, the federal government will do about the recession.
Ottawa could do three things:
Leave things alone and let the Canadian economy dip downward with the U.S. economy-
One gets the impression from reading the financial statement of the Minister of Finance of April 21, I think it was, the bootlegged statement he made-his first speech in this House; his second was last night, a five-minute speech that as usual told us nothing-that that was the course he was going to take. He said in the course of those remarks that we could not do much in Canada, that we are in the hands of the United States and had to follow them no matter where they go. That is one course. He continued with his second course as follows:
Try to prevent the recession from getting worse-
As the Liberal government did in 1974-75.
-by using the Keynesian techniques of tax cuts and government make-work projects-
That is another course the government could take except, of course, the government is already planning for a $14 billion deficit this year. The government has got itself in a straitjack-et with the deficits it plans for this year and the deficits it has racked up for the last eight years. It is going to be difficult for them to do that. They used the Keynesian techniques during all the good years. Now that they have used them through the good years they do not have them available to use during the bad years.
We are already in a morass of deficits and this year's is the largest yet. So can they do that? Are they going to attempt that? Is it not about time the government told this country and the financial community, the workers, the employers, which one of these alternatives they are going to try to take?
The third point was as follows:
Make the recession worse by following Britain's lead in tightening the money supply and cutting social programs to reduce the fiscal deficit.
That is another alternative. There are three alternatives. Later the author pointed out:
In fact, Mr. Trudeau's public statements so far indicate that he will attempt to duplicate the 1974-75 experience.
I say he probably would. He has no understanding of economics. Some of his statements would make your hair curl if you were not so busy laughing. Here is one of his statements. Back on April 24 at a press conference the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that the reason he wants to reduce the deficit is not to improve the health of the Canadian economy. He said it is healthy. The Prime Minister thinks the economy is healthy. Rather, he said, it is necessary to reduce the deficit because the interest charges on the deficit are so high due to high interest rates. The Prime Minister does not even see the connection between a higher deficit and more money that you have to pay in interest. That is the kind of rudimentary knowledge of economics that he demonstrates in this House.
In a February 14 campaign speech in Winnipeg the Prime Minister argued that the federal government should be doing the contrary to what the Conservatives planned in the Decern-
May 28, 1980

ber budget. When are they going to start doing the contrary, or to start doing anything in relation to economics and finances in this country?
The Minister of Finance said in response to a question that his policy and mine were the same. When is he going to clarify that statement? When is he going to give some leadership to this country as to where we are going? Is this the government that is going to do what the Prime Minister indicated during the campaign? I would say the odds are against it. He has not done a thing yet that he indicated during the campaign he would do.

These are some of the reasons why, before we approve a $12 billion and more borrowing by this government, we want to know what direction the government are going in and to what use they are going to put that money. Just what are they going to do? The Minister of Finance was reported as saying this on April 18. I have quoted this before in the House but it is so remarkable that I want to put it on the record again. In The Toronto Star for Friday, April 18-the Toronto black hole I call it-the Minister of Finance said:
__the lower rate was "welcome news", but it's worth pointing out that the high
interest rates we have had and the very rapid increases in these rates recently have been a direct result of action taken in the United States.
This was the same minister who got up here yesterday, patted himself on the back and pretended that there was some virtue of his that has resulted in interest rates dropping precipitously in the last several weeks, when on April 18 he admitted that the high interest rates that we have had have been a direct result of action taken in the United States. And, of course, the lower interest rates now are the same direct result. They have nothing to do with this Minister of Finance who answered a question yesterday with smart alec answers. We do not want smart alec answers. The 4,000 or 5,000 people who are going to be unemployed in the iron ore mines of Labrador in July do not want smart alec answers from this minister. They do want answers, but this is a minister who will not even answer. As I said last night, he is the silent butler of the government. He is the soft-shoe dancer. He is the soft-shoe specialist extraordinaire pit-patting down through the halls of power without giving us any answers. That has got to change. We are not satisfied with his soft-shoe techniques any more, Mr. Speaker.
Here is an article written by Ronald Anderson in The Globe and Mail who points out the sharp drop in interest rates. He writes:
Interest rates are moving down only because of a pronounced falling off in the demand for loans, especially for business loans in the United States. This, in itself, is a clear sign that the recession has arrived, and confirms the evidence of such other indicators.
Mr. Anderson goes on to examine the situation in the United States. Then he gives opinions from various financial houses and says that the weight of evidence indicates unmistakably that the North American recession will be severe
Borrowing Authority Act
rather than merely average, and so on. This will have its direct effects in Canada.
What position is the Minister of Finance and the government going to take on that? Are they going to reverse themselves again and adopt the same policy as was laid out in our budget-that you have to start getting the deficits down and under control over the next four or five years? You have to give more room to the private sector. They have not encouraged the private sector to build and grow, expand and employ more people; but you do have to stop borrowing so gigantically in the financial markets and give the private sector room to grow so it can borrow, grow and create jobs.
Is he going to take that route even though he voted against it? That is quite possible because since the government has assumed power he has gone all kinds of routes that he voted against on December 13. Is he going to do that, or is he going to take the 1974-75 lessons, ignore them, and go the other way as the Prime Minister indicates? He cannot have it both ways. What is he going to do? He should not just come to this House and ask for $12 billion and refuse to tell us or give us any indication of what he is going to do.
Just to give you the flavour, Mr. Speaker-

This caterwauling indicates why they are never going anywhere. They are going down the gopher holes out west in the next election.
Here is an indication of how the Minister of Finance treats this House. In Hansard on April 18, at page 160, the Minister of Finance was asked by me a question about the budget and oil pricing. This is what he said:
1 will certainly bring in a budget as soon as possible, but I do not see that possibility within the near future, or even beyond the near future.
This is as clear an answer as we ever get from that minister. He is going to bring in a budget as soon as possible, but he does not see the possibility within the near future, or even beyond the near future. We do not know if he even sees. I doubt that he sees. He certainly does not speak.
Then we move on to May 5 and we can see how informative he is on that day. The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) asked about financial assistance on wheat prices. Wheat prices are lower because of a decision made on embargoing grain shipments to the Soviet Union. This is the fulsome answer of the Minister of Finance at page 703 of Hansard:
Madam Speaker, 1 am not in a position to announce any immediate steps today but I shall take the hon. member's representation under consideration.

Not likely. Would the member for Prince Albert nod his head if he has heard from him? The hon. member is not nodding his head, so he has not heard from him since. The no nod NDP.
Now I will turn to Hansard for May 6, 1980, at page 742. This is why we are not rushing through $12 billion for somebody who cannot even speak or will not speak. The Minister of Finance was asked a question by the hon. member for St. John's West, who does not often get a chance in this House to ask. At page 741 of Hansard, the Minister of Finance was asked this:
-will the minister advise the House what steps the government is taking to increase real domestic output, manufacturing output, and employment in Canada this year, particularly in view of the forecasts-
That is for Ontario. Ontario is having a bad time economically. I know, Mr. Speaker, that you are amazed to hear that, coming from Ottawa, but it is true.
The Deputy Prime Minister was then asked a supplementary question about the Canadian dollar. In answer to that question he said this at page 742:
My hon. friend knows that the Canadian dollar is reacting to market forces at the present time.
That the Canadian dollar is reacting was a real nugget. The final supplementary question reads as follows:
Is the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance satisfied with the present level of the value of the Canadian dollar, and is his policy to keep it at the present level of value or is he prepared to allow it to rise?
The answer to that question is as follows:
Madam Speaker, the Canadian dollar has fluctuated rather widely in the last two months.
Then I interjected with the following:
So have you.

Then the Minister of Finance goes on to say:
The governor of the Bank has permitted that fluctuation to take place, and 1 believe that is a comment in itself to the hon. member.
That is a great answer, that the governor of the Bank of Canada has enabled it to take place, and that that is a comment itself. The Minister of State for Finance is here today listening with rapt attention, and I congratulate him for that because he is not going to get a chance to listen to his minister who does not say very much. But when we ask a serious question about the economic and financial future of this country, these are the kinds of answers we get from the Minister of Finance.
Again, on May 21, 1980-I am only giving a rapid selection because I do not have much time to speak today-in Hansard at page 1256, another question was put to the Minister of Finance. This time the question was raised by the hon.
member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) about a $1 billion saving the minister is going to get from the blended price system. The Minister of Finance replied in this way:
I can only tell the hon. member that the blended price system can achieve results, but the greater the increase in international prices, the greater the difficulty.
That is a fulsome answer when he is asked to explain how he can save $1 billion. In answer to a supplementary question about commitments made in his April 21 economic statement, the Minister of Finance said this:
With respect to the question as to what is now the precise burden of the oil import compensation program, I would be pleased to get those updated figures and make them available to the House and to the hon. member.
Has the Minister of Finance got those updated figures and made them available to the House and the hon. member? He has not. He answered the question here in the House that day and then he softshoes out of the House, down the halls, going down to get those prices which he forgot about and which we have never seen since. We turn the page to page 1259 and the Minister of Finance is asked by the member for St. John's West the following:
It was announced in Newfoundland yesterday that Wabush mine, which operates an iron ore mine in Labrador, has suffered a 15 per cent loss of sales of its product to the United States this year because of depression or recession in the United States, and as a result for one month-the month of July-all of its workers are going to be laid off or have to go on their holidays. What steps is the Minister taking to try to overcome such effects of the recession in the United States as are now becoming evident in Canada? What steps is he taking to overcome these effects?
I consider that to be a serious question, not just a light question, not just a little question to get up on your feet and exercise yourself getting up and down. There is going to be 1,500 people out of work. Since then we have the news of another 4,000 in Labrador city. Here is the answer given by the Minister of Finance to that question:
With respect to the workers affected by the lay-off, as the hon. member knows, they will be able to take advantage of programs especially in place at the present time.
And so on. He went on to say:
In connection with the recession that may be taking place and is undoubtedly beginning in the United States-
A great admission by this minister.
-the hon. member raises a question that is very broad indeed.
That is very informative. It tells the House that I have raised a question that is very broad. The minister continues:
As he knows, there are only, in a sense, two ways that one can act in circumstances of this kind; that is, through increased spending or through reduced taxes in order to stimulate the Canadian economy. 1 have not yet reached the conclusion that that is an appropriate stance to take at the present time.
Do you get that, Mr. Speaker? Pure and utter bafflegab; pure and utter vacuity; pure and utter lack of information. This is a government that has been in place 86 days, that ejected us from power and that used every pragmatic means-
I will call it that because I am going to be statesmanlike this afternoon-to get back in power themselves. They disagreed
May 28, 1980

with our budget. They thought it was shocking and frightening.
When the minister is asked 80 days after he got into government what he is going to do to meet the U.S. recession, he does not know. He tells us there are several options: we can increase spending or reduce taxes. We already knew that. Every simpleton in Canada knows you can increase taxes or reduce taxes or increase spending or reduce spending. We do not need a Minister of Finance to bafflegab and flap that past us in the House when we ask a question. He says he has not reached a conclusion which is appropriate at the present time. Well, we have not reached a conclusion as to whether $12 billion is appropriate for borrowing authority for this minister at the present time, not until he comes into this House and starts to tell the people of Canada and the members of this House what his economic and financial approach is going to be.
We want a budget and we want a firm date set for a budget. We know there is going to be an oil price war. We have seen the attitude of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) outside this House and repeated here today. He is looking for nothing but war and confrontation with the oil producing provinces and many of the people of this country. He gets up and says he has just won a successful battle against separatism in Quebec and now he has to fight another battle. He implies it is another battle against separatism, only this time in Alberta and with the oil producing provinces.
He is the man who is supposed to go out and negotiate for this government a successful conclusion to this whole oil price and energy price difficulty that we have had for the last year. We can see now what he plans to do. He plans to have war and confrontation with Alberta, hoping that he can rally the rest of the country around him on the ground that we need a strong central government to deal with the separatist threat in the west.
This man will put this country in peril just to try to achieve the carrying out of cheap political promises made last fall and winter to this country, and he knows he cannot carry them out any other way. He knows he can only carry them out if he unilaterally imposes new taxes on the oil and gas industry and takes the money from the producing provinces and the industry. This is the stage he is sitting. His tactic is beneath belief. It is unconscionable.

Yes, it is a dishonest approach. How can anyone going out to really try and negotiate with a group of people a very contentious question like this and make statements so insulting, so calculated to make the blood boil? The Prime Minister of this country endorses this attitude. He should be ashamed of himself.
To come back a bit more to the topic, let me look at the debate of October 23, 1979, when I asked this House for borrowing authority of $7 billion for the rest of 1980, to expire on March 31, 1980. What did gentlemen opposite do? They spoke on that bill. I had to borrow the money to meet their
Borrowing Authority Act
obligations to carry out their budget. It was not mine. I was asking the House for $7 billion to carry out their programs, their financial system and their budget of the previous November, and what did they do? They talked for four days. We had nine Liberal speakers and seven NDP speakers. They will speak on anything, that crowd in the NDP. They will speak on anything, any time they get a chance, God bless them. They are great speakers. There were two PC speakers. We had four days of debate, the 23rd, 25th, 26th and 29th, on second reading.
There was a long interruption caused by the hon. member for somewhere or other down in New Brunswick. The hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) moved the adjournment of the House. A couple of hours were lost because nobody was here; nobody anticipated this resolute action by that fighter for civil liberties, the honourable Breau. That is the kind of thing that went on when we asked this House for $7 billion last fall.
We heard also from the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray). We do not see him around too much these days. I guess he has gone up the spout somewhere with Chrysler. He seems to have them and only them on his mind. The then finance critic is up the tailpipe.
The then finance critic said we only needed $3.5 billion. We did not need $7 billion; we only needed $3.5 billion. Therefore we have ample precedent just a few months ago as to what to do with this bill. We have serious purpose behind this objection we are taking to this bill because we are going to carry out the advice that they gave us last October 23. Let me just briefly refer to some of it. I am referring to Hansard, for those of you who have not looked recently. The hon. member for Windsor West complained about interest rates and so on. He has forgotten it all now. He is thrilled with the interest rates since. He said that we bore the responsibility for the damage the interest rate increases were doing to small business, the farmer and the consumer. When this government got in, interest rates went up 2.2 per cent. That is how much he cared. He said this at page 509:
But there is another serious flaw in the way the Conservatives are proceeding with this first financial measure they have called for debate in this new Parliament. They are seeking this $7 billion in borrowing authority in Bill C-10 without first presenting their own budget to Parliament.
He was seriously upset. The "honourable Herbie" was seriously upset that we had not presented a budget and we deigned to ask for $7 billion in borrowing authority to carry out their spending plans. There is our serious flaw. I give this advice to the Minister of Finance. He has got a serious flaw in asking us for $12 billion because he is seeking it without first presenting a budget to Parliament. What's sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander.
We want to see a budget before the end of June. We will then give the government the $12 billion if we think it is a worth-while budget. If we do not think it is a worth-while budget, they will have to claw us, fight for it, impose closure and rack it up and down the House and out in the corridors to get it. But don't be afraid to bring in a budget. All that can happen is they might be defeated.

May 28, 1980
Borrowing Authority Act

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Let me give them another piece of advice that we got in that debate from the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien). He said this. He understood my problem. He urged me to talk to the then prime minister and make sure that the oil and gas pricing problem was resolved very quickly. Good advice, Mr. Minister. 1 am glad to see that M. le Ministre of Energy, Mines and Resources is buckling right down to settling this question very quickly. We saw that last night. He will need tanks to settle the question. He will need artillery to settle it if he is going to proceed as he did last night. That is the only way he is going to settle it. There is no agreement between two consenting parties. There is not going to be any agreement between two consenting adults in private or in public if he continues as he was acting last night and this afternoon.
What else was the good advice from the former minister of finance? He said this. He was all caught up about a budget and he said this at page 516:
-so that the people could make plans for the year to come on the basis of a budget that would be known to everybody.
He asked this question:
How can they prepare against inflation next year without knowing the government's budgetary intentions?
I ask the same question of the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister, who 1 know is not listening and will not pay any attention anyway. How can the people of Canada prepare against inflation? How can they prepare against anything when they do not know what this government's budgetary intentions are? They have been frightened to death and frightened out of their wits by the $14 billion deficit already indicated by the Minister of Finance, but they have had no indication yet as to how the government is going to tackle our economic problems.
At page 517 the former minister of finance was talking about the difference in their approach compared to ours, and he said this:
We do not think it is necessary to let the Canadian economy go into a recession as the Americans have. We managed to prove that point in 1974 and 1975, and 1 hope that the Minister of Finance will keep that in mind.
That is the belief of the former minister of finance. We do not know the belief of the present Minister of Finance. When is he going to let Canada know? When are the manufacturers going to know what the prospects are with this government? These are some of the questions we have.
Here is Mr. Carl Beigie outlining an economic plan. Canada needs a co-ordinated strategy to reduce consumer spending and raise investments as much as it needs national unity, according to Mr. Beigie, who is the president of the C. D. Howe Research Institute. This is what we read in a clipping from The Globe and Mail of May 22, 1980. He was speaking to a group of economists in Montreal. He proposed action on five key points-more cuts in government spending, a willingness to allow prices to rise faster so as to discourage consumer spending and encourage investment, more taxes on consumer spending, a set of measures to reward productive investment and measures to punish the use of capital for dividend increases, mergers and acquisitions. The final recommendation is maintenance of the dollar at a level favouring sectors other than non-renewable resources.
Those are the suggestions of one economist as to what should be done at the moment. There are dozens more. People engaged in the industries of this country along with the farmers and fishermen need to know in which direction the government is going. But all we hear from the Minister of Finance is that he cannot make a move until there is an oil pricing agreement. He can make assumptions. There will be no oil pricing agreement. I make that forecast now, Mr. Speaker. Certainly there will be no agreement by July unless the government has a plot, as I now suspect it has, to start a war with the province of Alberta and the other provinces which possess resources, and then impose a unilateral solution. But there is going to be no agreement.
Here are some of the questions to which we need answers from the minister. This is some of the information we should be getting. There are two ways for the government to secure borrowing authority. One is from Parliament, and the government is now asking for authority under this bill. That is new money. But the government has continuing authority to borrow funds to repay maturing debt. What we want to know is: How much authority do they now have in view of the fact that they have been repaying maturing debt over recent months? We know they had to redeem more than $1 billion in Canada savings bonds. That gives them authority to borrow another billion without coming to the House at all. So let the minister tell us what he has under that heading.
We know that all their authority under the bill passed last fall expired on April 1. But the usage of borrowing powers is calculated on a net basis, so that as the government reduces the level of outstanding debt it increases its borrowing power. On November 1, 1979, there was $2.9 billion of unused borrowing authority still outstanding, available to be carried forward. The minister has stated that this was still the case on April 1. So let us have the facts on that. Imagine coming to this House for authority to raise $12 billion and the minister doesn't even tell us how he plans to get it-how much by way of Canada Savings Bonds, how much by way of marketable bonds, how much by way of treasury bills. How does he plan to borrow this $12 billion? What is his borrowing plan? He makes a five-minute speech during which he tells the House nothing. He doesn't tell us how much will come from government pension funds, how much is expected to come from the public market-
