speechtext: Or at what rate.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
-or what rate he expects to pay. We want some information on that. What does the government intend to do about Canada Savings Bonds? A huge proportion of our debt is represented by Canada Savings Bonds. The people who
May 28, 1980

hold those bonds could come in tomorrow and ask for payment. What would the government do about that? The government says it will reduce its reliance on Canada Savings Bonds and if members over there are not going to do it, they are making a bad mistake.
Just look at the proportion here. It is something like 18 per cent to 20 per cent of our indebtedness, if not more. In the first several months of this year, $1.1 billion were redeemed, an amount equal to the whole of last year. In a moment, looking through these notes, I will come across the proportion of government debt which is in Canada Savings Bonds. It is a very high percentage. The government must get out of that. The people are getting worried about their interest rates, worried about inflation and we may yet see the whole kit and caboodle, widows and all, coming in next week with $18 billion worth of Canada Savings Bonds to be cashed.
What is the government going to do if that occurs? It might not be $18 billion, it might be only half that amount, $9 billion. It might be a quarter, $3 billion or $4 billion. We cannot continue with so high a proportion of our debt in Canada Savings Bonds. Does the Minister of Finance intend to explain what he is going to do to avoid trouble and difficulty in that direction? Is that not his responsibility when he comes to the House for authority to borrow $12 billion? Does he think the members on his own side are dum-dums, dodos or greenbacks who would not be interested in this information? Does he think they are uncaring? I see a number of members over there who are caring. Others are passed caring-the ones who have been there any length of time. But the rest of them are still caring. Shouldn't they have this information? Shouldn't the members of the cabinet have it?
This is the kind of information we want. We want to know how much of our indebtedness is in treasury bills, how much in one year bills, how much in Canada Savings Bonds, how much in bonds altogether. What is our present debt as of today, or as of May 15 or some reasonable date? How is it held? How much is on short term, how much is on long term and the rest?
According to my little black book, back in October when this estimate was done, interest charges for 1980-81 were expected to be $10.5 billion. That has since gone up to $10,750 million. The gross public debt charges as a percentage of total government outlays were 18.2 per cent. The figure is higher, now.
I remember when I was minister of finance in Newfoundland. The minister of finance of the mighty Liberal government, which was almost solvent in those days, back in 1972, was advising me that Newfoundland was headed for bankruptcy if we continued to borrow in the way we were borrowing. That is when the borrowing started here. It went up from $1,253 billion in 1972 to total $46.5 billion over the next seven years. It quadrupled from the time the Prime Minister took office in 1968. Now, 18.2 per cent of all government outlay is going to pay public debt charges and the minister comes to this House with the thought that we are going to give him $12 billion borrowing authority. And he gives us no information. What is the interest cost to Canada going to be, Mr. "Assist-
Borrowing Authority Act
ant Minister of Finance"? What is the latest estimate for 1980-81 of what the interest on gross public debt is going to be? What percentage will that be of total government outlays and what percentage will it be of the gross national product? The Prime Minister of Canada might not care about the deficit, but I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that it is very, very important. The people of Canada, or their children, will rue the day that this kind of thing went on. It is our duty to ask questions and look to the future. So we want some information about these matters.
It was originally thought that in 1980 the interest cost, the cost of the public debt program, would be $8,350 million. That is what was in the Main Estimates prepared by the same government which sits opposite now. That was an 18.3 per cent increase over the previous year's level, 1978-79. Well, then the estimate went up from $8,350 million to $8,450 million, an increase of 19.7 per cent over the previous year. That happened during the year and the estimate had to be revised. The latest note I have here is that last October we expected the interest costs for last year to go to $8,600 million, or 21.8 per cent above the previous year. What was the figure? What did it finally turn out to be? The last estimate I had was that it was going to cost us 21.8 per cent more for interest in 1979-80 than it had cost us in 1978-79.
We want that information, Mr. Speaker, before we pass this bill. The minister will just have to be more forthcoming. The people of Canada want to know what is happening with these tremendous increases in interest costs.
There is a note here also that the balance outstanding in employee pension accounts continues to increase, accounting for a major source of government financing. A lot of the government's financing now is coming from compulsory acquisitions of funds from government pension accounts, moneys paid in by public servants and other people paid from the public treasury. They are compulsorily having to lend that money from their pension funds to the Government of Canada to reduce the amount the government has to go to the markets for. How much is that going to be for the present year? What is the latest forecast on that? What are they going to be able to take from non-government sources, from government pension funds and the like? We would like to know. We would like to know how much of the Canadian debt now is payable in Canadian dollars and how much of it is payable in foreign currency. That would be of interest. The last figures I have here are that at October 31, 1979, we had a total government debt of $68,067 billion. Of that, $63,144 billion was in Canadian dollar debt, and the remainder was in foreign currency debt, the Deutschmark, the Japanese yen, the Swiss franc.
There is nowhere that this government will not borrow. They will go anywhere in this world to borrow. Their next loan will probably be in the old Zambian Kwacha or whatever. We would like to know what these figures are now for the latest period we have them for before we go authorizing another $12 billion. How much of their domestic debt program last year is

May 28, 1980
Borrowing Authority Act
held by the Bank of Canada? How much are they planning to have the Bank of Canada hold for this year? Last year, at least up until October 31, the Bank of Canada had financed Government of Canada cash requirements to the extent of $1.2 billion. What did this turn out to be for the whole year? What are their plans for using Bank of Canada financing this year? That has an important effect on inflation, the money supply and the like.
These are some of the questions we expect to have answered, and they are not unreasonable, surely, when this House is asked to approve $12 billion in borrowing authority. What are the interest costs on the foreign debt? The gross annual interest cost on foreign loans for March, 1978, outstanding as of October 31, amounted to U.S. $326 million. What is it now? What are the net interest costs? What are they earning on those proceeds? These are some of the questions the Minister of Finance or his Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) might find that if they answered we would be co-operative in trying to get this bill through the House before we adjourn in July, August or September.
What is the government's fiscal plan? What is the government going to do? How much is the oil import compensation plan now going to cost? What is the latest figure on that? It was $3.1 billion, but now we have had increases in the price charged by foreign countries in connection with our oil imports, so what is it going to be now? These are some of the things we want information on.
I do not believe I have forgotten any questions. I know some of our speakers will have further questions, and that is all to the good.
Now, what are some of the things that the people of Canada are concerned about and want to get information about? They want to know what the government is going to do, and this government will not tell them.
According to a report I have here, in two decades of surveying consumer attitudes the Conference Board in Canada has never found Canadians to be as pessimistic as they are now. That is what the board said on May 22. They have been doing these surveys. They did a quarterly survey of consumer confidence, and they find that Canadians are showing increasing concern about their families' financial prospects, about employment possibilities, about making major purchases at this time.
Well, if consumers are the gloomiest they have been in two decades, surely it is up to the government to try to reinstil some confidence in the consumer by telling the consumer what the government's plans are and how they foresee the year. If the government cannot do anything and if the government's hands are tied because of its present huge deficit and its present huge deficit in the balance of international payments, the government cannot go into expansionary spending or increase the deficit beyond the $14 billion. I myself cannot see how they could do that. It would be very dangerous and damaging. If they cannot do it, they should tell the people of Canada that they cannot, and about what we have to prepare for and how they see us coming out of it.
According to the board, for the first quarter of 1980 the index was 82.7, one of the lowest levels measured since the surveys began in 1960. Well, is to ask this House for borrowing authority of $12 billion without any information or indication of the government's financial and economic plans going to induce confidence in the consumer? You bet it is not, Mr. Speaker.
Here is another clipping. One does not have to be a genius to read the papers and see the result of these surveys. Canada has the worst productivity in the seven major free world nations. We had a decline of productivity last year from 1978 levels. The U.S. had the lowest gain, but they had a gain. But Canada had a loss. Canada had a decline in productivity, 0.8 per cent. Italy had an increase of 8.7 per cent; Japan, 8.3 per cent; France, 5.4 per cent; Germany, 5.2 per cent; Great Britain, so often sneered at and looked down on, had increased productivity of 2.2 per cent. Canada had a "decline" of 0.8 per cent. What is the government's plan to help deal with that situation? The government has been in office for 16 years with a brief interruption of eight or nine months. They are back in office again. What is their plan to deal with that?
When the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce was finance critic for the then opposition, he was full of plans as to how he was going to overcome all these things.
According to another report, the decline in our buying power is the worst since the depression. This comes from Statistics Canada. Canadians' purchasing power has declined steadily in the last three years. It is the worst drop since the depression of the early 1930s, according to Statistics Canada. How long does the Minister of Finance think this decline in our buying power is going to go on? Does he see this stopping this year or next year? Is there anything he can do about it?
The whole history of collective bargaining in this country will be affected by the expectation of the labour unions as to whether their buying power is going to continue to decline or not. Can the minister not bring in a budget and give them some indication of where he expects this situation to go? What is the long-term outlook if we are restraining ourselves now and our buying power is declining now? Are we going to be better off in the future? If we tighten our belt now, are we going to be better off a year, two years or three years down the road?
These are questions the people of Canada want answered. They do not want the minister to be mute on these questions. They do not want him to be sliding and skating all through the question period refusing to answer any questions, just talking. He is a very skilled parliamentarian. We all know that this Minister of Finance can avoid answering questions. We know that if he is not the most skilful, he is one of the most skilful parliamentarians in this chamber. That does not mean that he is to be admired for refusing to answer questions when he is the Minister of Finance.
The President of the CMA, Mr. Newall, spoke recently. He said, and I am quoting from a report in The Globe and Mail of
May 27:
May 28, 1980

-if government will provide the right climate, manufacturing industry can invest between $150 billion and $200 billion in larger and more productive plants this decade.
The pertinent words here are "if government will provide the right climate". Most people do not expect that this government will provide the right climate. The budget of December 11 did provide the right climate, a climate for people to invest with confidence that they were going to get a return on their money, that they were going to be able to employ more people and that we were freeing up the private sector to some degree so that they could get on with the job of doing what they know best-removing the dead hand of the government.
That is not the attitude this government has been known for in the past, and it does not sound as if it is going to be in the future, so is the government going to provide the right climate? What climate are they going to provide for our manufacturing industry? We can only know that when we have a budget. That is the only time we are going to know that. We are not going to know by giving the government the right to borrow another $12 billion.
Here is the C.D. Howe Research Institute again making a report. This is May 2 in The Globe and Mail again.
Canada will not begin to solve its inflation problem until the federal government's deficit is reduced, according to Carl Beigie-
Mr. Beigie, again, is the president of the C.D. Howe Research Institute.
In Canada surplus demand originates primarily in the government sector through budgetary deficits.
And so on. I will not read it all into the record, but it is true. It is correct. Mr. Beigie and I believe that the federal deficit is the key to inflation. Is this government going to do anything about inflation? Are we going to feel safe to save money or not? Is it going to become too dangerous for people in this country to save money because the government does not care about inflation or it will not fight inflation or will not take the painful steps that are necessary to fight inflation? This government has now got a safe majority for the next four or five years. It does not take any courage to fight inflation when you have a safe majority.
We made the decision that we were going to fight it when we did not have a majority. I suppose that in political terms that was a mistake, but the government now has a majority. When is it going to indicate to the people of this country, to the people who have some money to save, to the people whose money is needed to be invested in this country, whether or not it is safe for them to save it, or should they all shoot outdoors today and spend it before it loses even more of its value? That is the main question.
The bill which we passed in the House yesterday giving $35 per household to help those who receive a guaranteed income supplement to the old age pension is a picayune measure. That $35 might help them temporarily, but what helps the old age pensioner, the older person and those on fixed incomes is not that kind of small token, a handout from the government, or
Borrowing Authority Act
whatever it is, an attempt to give them security. The only security they will have is if we overcome inflation so that their cost of living will not go up by 10 per cent, 12 per cent or 15 per cent every year. We must ensure that this country does not go bust, that we do not wreck the economy. The only security anyone has in this country is if we operate the economy properly and we produce more so there is more to divide among us all and we give more to the senior citizens and the rest.
A party that is not interested in the fight against inflation, that will not battle inflation, is not interested in the older people, the senior citizens, is not interested in the dispossessed, is not interested in those who do not have strong organizations to protect them. The people of Canada want to know: is this government going to fight inflation? Because we have no indication whether or not they are. The minister's statement of April 21 indicates they are not. He is satisfied with a deficit of $14 billion.
The United States, whose interest rates and everything else the minister is following, are going the other way; they will have a small surplus next year in their budget. If they adopted the same policies we have and followed us-our deficit is $14 billion-they would have a deficit ten times that size amounting to $140 billion, yet they are going to balance their budget next year to try to fight inflation.
What is this government going to do? It is not telling us. All we have had is this pitiful excuse, this document which was presented to us on April 21 which we were not allowed to debate.
As I mentioned a few moments ago, we have a Prime Minister who thinks we have a healthy economy. Well, we should have the world's healthiest economy. We have the possibilities for a healthy economy, but we have an economy which has been badly mismanaged for the last ten years at least. For nine months we made a beginning in trying to get it back again to a healthy state. Now we do not know whether this government will follow that direction or go on to complete the dismantling of our economy which they proceeded to do from 1972 to 1979.
I believe that the Prime Minister is the Count Dracula of the Canadian economic system. The Prime Minister has to start giving it a transfusion, giving it more power, not just taking the blood out of it. His government has been like Dracula, like a vampire bat feeding on the economic system of Canada for the last seven or eight years. Are they going to stop that and start giving the economy a transfusion, or will they continue taking all the life blood out of it? That is the question which the Minister of Finance will not even answer.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: He is not even here.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
The Minister has had to go somewhere outside the country, I believe. But the Minister of State for Finance is here and I think that he is the man concerned with these questions and he might put them to the Minister of Finance.

May 28, 1980
Borrowing Authority Act
The Prime Minister remarked on our healthy economy. At the same time, on April 21, here is how the Minister of Finance spoke about the health of our economy. He said inflation appears worse now than in the previous peak inflation years of 1974 and 1975. That is one point he made. He said also that the underlying rates of inflation in the United States and Canada are not very different. He said the consumer price index will rise by 10 per cent this year. He said there will be little or no growth in Canada in 1980. He said that residential construction is likely to decline. He said that Canada cannot insulate itself from the slowdown in the United States because of the substantial deficit which already exists on the current account of our balance of payments and because of the size of the already existing deficit of the federal government. That statement is the exact opposite of the statement made by the present Minister of Justice on October 23 when he was in opposition, and which I quoted earlier.
The Minister of Finance said that the unemployment rate would rise this year to an average of 8 per cent. Does the Prime Minister think that is healthy? Does he think that all these things are healthy?
As I just mentioned, the Conference Board has found Canadians never to have been so pessimistic before. The productivity situation is not good, our purchasing power has declined. But the Prime Minister says our economy is healthy. He does not worry about deficits, except that they cost more in interest. He is worried because interest costs are higher. All this is not calculated to reassure the people of this country that their serious economic problems will receive much attention, if any.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, as the first speaker 1 have unlimited time. As the opposition spokesman on the government bill I was hoping to address myself to this bill for three or four days to review in depth what the government needs to do and what the problems are. But I have to take a plane to Toronto this afternoon to fulfil a commitment to speak there tonight, and therefore I cannot take the time I want on this bill. But eventually this bill will go to committee.
I suggest to the Minister of State for Finance that when he speaks-and I am sure he will be speaking-he give us some of the basic information we want. If we can get some sense from the government on what their economic and financial plans are, we are willing to give the government borrowing authority. It might be $12 billion or less than that, depending on what the government shows it needs. It depends on the government telling us what its plans are and telling the Canadian people. If the government can show at any time that there is some emergency, that they cannot meet a cheque, that they cannot meet the social security payments, or something like that, because they cannot borrow the money, they do not have that authority, if they can show that then we will be agreeable to rush through $1 billion or $2 billion of borrowing authority, some reasonable amount. But the government is not so down in the mouth, so financially strapped, that it cannot carry on its operations because we will not give it borrowing authority. We will give it some borrowing authority, but the official opposition will not agree to give $12 billion borrowing authority blind. We are not like the three blind mice. We want to see some evidence of the government's serious intentions and actions.
We want to have information. We will not be shoved around here by the government. Perhaps the electorate does not worry at present. They do not appear to be following public affairs with any great attention. This might be the case now, but they will not always be like this. I have been here only since 1976 and I thought I had seen some arrogance exhibited by the government up to May of 1979, but what I have seen in this House since April 14 shows that in the few brief months that they were out of office no new attitudes at all have been adopted.
The government thinks it has a majority and does not need to worry about anything. It thinks that the memory of the public is so short that the public will not remember in three months' time what the government is doing or not doing today. It made solemn commitments to mortgage holders, to the renters of Canada, to home owners. It told them that we were not doing enough. They were in this chamber and they opposed our mortgage tax credit legislation. They fought it bitterly in this chamber. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) when he was in the opposition wept crocodile tears and said that we were not helping renters, we were not helping the lower income people.
During the campaign, they went on with the same line. They stopped our attempt to help the home owner, the poor person burdened with mortgage costs, and they pretended that the high interest costs were our fault. When they came into office they allowed those costs to go even higher to 16.2 per cent for the bank rate and 17 per cent or 18 per cent on mortgages. Now, luckily for them and for everyone, the rates are coming down because of the recession, for no other reason. They promised the people of Canada they would help the home owner, the renter and the mortgage holder. They have not done a thing in their 86 days in power.
This House has been sitting since April 14 and the government has done nothing but give excuses for not helping the renters of Canada, not helping the mortgage holders of Canada. Ministers are still saying they are going to help 4,000, 5,000 or 6,000 people who got involved in AHOP and have been put in a terrible position over that program. They now have to renew their mortgages after five years at double and triple what the costs were originally and they cannot afford it. The government says it may still help them, but those are the only people it is going to help in Canada. These are the people who made the welkin ring in this House last fall about how their hearts bled for the Canadian home owner and the Canadian renter, yet they have done nothing since they got into power. They have offered no legislation to this House and they do not explain now why they opposed what we did offer. They could have supported that and improved it, if they thought there should be improvements, when they got into
May 28, 1980

power. They think the people of Canada have very short memories. Perhaps they are right, but they are taking an awful chance. If the people of Canada have got short memories, we are going to be here to remind them about some of the things the government promised and committed but which it is now not doing.
They are trying to fool the people on oil pricing. They have blended prices; they have "blanded" prices. They have the best kinds of prices. They have a new electric blender over in the Prime Minister's office and he is getting all the stuff and he is blending it all up, and they are going to try to convince the Canadian people that prices will not have gone up more than they were going up under our policy-$4 a barrel this year and $4.50 next year. We will be revealing how that is not so as they try to unfold that program.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, if he was Pinocchio, would have a nose that would reach from here to Vancouver with the stories he has told on energy pricing since he became the minister on March 3. If the Canadian people are not listening too intently now we intend to see that the record is clear so that when they do take an interest they will see what we were trying to accomplish and how, and what this government promised and what it has done, which are two distinctly different things.
By the way, 1 have a final note here. This is a final piece of arrogance and 1 have not received an apology for this yet. Here is a document sent out by 74 of the Liberal MPs from Quebec to householders in Quebec just before the referendum vote. This one here is from the MP for Vercheres (Mr. Loiselle). It shows a separated Quebec gone from Canada, and gone with Quebec is 110,000 square miles of Newfoundland and Labrador. Not only that, Newfoundland is pushed out 200 miles into the Atlantic Ocean. It is no wonder Premier Peck-ford said you should only be the agents for the provinces. In this brochure you have pushed the island out 200 miles into the Atlantic and you took Labrador away from it, showing it going off with a separated Quebec.
Every one of the 74 members from Quebec, as far as I know, sent that brochure out. We have not heard a word yet to say it was a mistake, that they did not mean to include the 110,000 square miles of Newfoundland with Quebec. Perhaps they did not want to show the true boundary because there was a sensitive election going on. Maybe that was the reason. We call that arrogance down in Newfoundland.
My God, there is so much to talk about, Mr. Speaker, why do I have to leave? We have a Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who said in a brave speech in Toronto when he was again threatening Alberta on May 6, and this appears at page 3 of his speech:
There will be free flow of goods and services in this country. No province has the right to dictate development outside its borders, and the federal government will fully defend this basic constitutional principle.
That is what he said in Toronto. When he is asked in this House whether he will apply that principle to Newfoundland and Labrador so there can be a free flow of hydroelectricity from Labrador to other provinces in Canada across Quebec,
Borrowing Authority Act
which is now stopped by Quebec which will not permit it unless the power is sold to it at the price it sets so it can resell it at a far greater price and make fast profits, while we hewers of wood and drawers of water in Newfoundland make nothing, they do not assure us that they will apply that principle in the province of Quebec.
This is the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who has so flexed his muscles now with Alberta he is "super Marc"; he is going to crush Alberta; he is going to crush Lougheed. He says the principle is:
No province has the right to dictate development outside its borders, and the federal government will fully defend this basic constitutional principle.
When Newfoundland and Labrador asked him to defend that principle against Quebec, Newfoundland with seven seats and the province of Quebec with 75, that is the last we hear of it. They turn and they twist every way you can think of in the House here to avoid answering that question. That question will be coming up when the Lower Churchill studies are finished in the next couple of weeks. That question will then be right in the lap of the federal government, because those developments cannot go ahead; the Lower Churchill cannot be developed with a potential 2,500 megawatts of power badly needed in the maritimes to displace oil. That cannot go ahead unless Newfoundland can transmit that power across Quebec to these other provinces. That problem will be right in their laps, and that great principle will have to be followed or revealed to be a completely hollow principle.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, let me just say that the requests we are making are reasonable. When you look at the way the debt and the borrowing have increased in Canada, it just makes your head spin, particularly the way it has happened in the last ten years. We now have a situation where the House is being asked to authorize $12 billion in borrowing authority. There was one period of two years when the amount was $28 billion. This is given in my briefing book which says "net debt borrowed", and there was borrowed $28 billion in 1977-78 and 1978-79. Now the government is asking for $12 billion. These are huge amounts of money.
The man who asks the House for this authority spoke last night for five minutes, filling just one page of Hansard. The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance can treat this bill so lightly that all he thinks he has to do is ask the House to give him the right to borrow $12 billion without a word of explanation as to why he wants it, how he is going to raise it, what his present authorities are and the like. This just boggles the imagination. He treats the matter very lightly, just as the minister has treated us in respect of the questions we asked in the House. It is not a question of whether we like the Minister of Finance or whether we do not like him. I personally like him. I have a high regard for his ability to do the old soft-shoe dance. I call him "old slippery heels". But he is going to get caught. He cannot be Minister of Finance and avoid answering all the questions. He cannot be Minister of Finance and avoid telling the people of Canada what his approach is going to be to the economy and the financial system of Canada for the next two or three years. He cannot do that without ruinous effects to our economy.

May 28, 1980
Borrowing Authority Act
It may be that the Minister of State for Finance will repair all the damage of the Minister of Finance when he speaks. I think he is the back-up man for the Minister of Finance. I think the Prime Minister knows that the Minister of Finance is not too forthcoming so he has got the Minister of State for Finance to back the minister up and do the things he is not going to do. We hope that is the case. In the meantime we are prepared to explore these issues and discuss every aspect of government operation in the coming weeks until the government does become more forthcoming and, particularly, until we find out when there is going to be a budget, or, in the alternative, what this government's approach is to our economic and financial problems about which they were so anxious to defeat us. Perhaps they defeated us just because they were anxious to get into power again. I think that is the true reason; I think that is the only reason. If that is not the reason they should be eager to come into this House and show us how they are going to go right when we were going so wrong. That is what we want the minister to do before we give him this authority to borrow another $12 billion.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are being asked through the provisions of this bill to permit the Government of Canada to borrow $12 billion for the fiscal year 1980-81. As I listened to the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) outline the reasons he was bringing forth this bill in his very brief speech yesterday, I did not know whether to laugh or to cry. I remember that this is the finance minister who engineered the defeat of the Conservative government last December. This is the finance minister who persuaded the Fiberal members of Parliament last December to vote for the NDP motion which led to the defeat of the Conservative government. This is the finance minister who, according to the most knowledgeable media people, persuaded or forced all Liberal MPs to be here in this House to vote on that fateful day last December. This is the finance minister who, we are told, persuaded the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to stay on in politics. This is the finance minister who, having moved from the opposition benches to take his portfolio, seems to have forgotten all the pledges made by his leader and his party before the last election and during the last election campaign.
This is the finance minister who has implemented all of the measures proposed by the former Conservative finance minister last December, except for the 18-cent a gallon excise tax. This is the finance minister who obviously believes that the government should not interfere actively in directing the economy, either to get it moving at a faster rate or to slow it down. This is the most silent finance minister I have ever seen in my 18 years of Parliament.
Under the regime of this finance minister we will see a situation in the coming year in which growth will be restricted to just a 1 per cent increase in the gross national product, according to the Conference Board in Canada. The cost of
living will increase by 10 per cent or more if the price of oil moves up as the province of Alberta wishes, and unemployment will undoubtedly increase by at least a half to 1 per cent in the next year over what it was in the last year.
I would like to remind members on the government side that on December 13, 1979, their party voted for an amendment moved by the New Democratic Party to their amendment on the budget of the Conservative party. That vote led to the end of the Conservative government. Our amendment was supported by the Liberal party, so we assumed that they endorsed its principles. Our amendment was:
-and this House unreservedly condemns the government for its outright betrayal of its election promises to lower interest rates, to cut taxes, and to stimulate the growth of the Canadian economy, without a mandate from the Canadian people for such a reversal.
When the Conservatives were in power, the interest rate was approximately 11.5 per cent. In the few months in which the Liberal government has been in power, it went up to approximately 17 per cent. Of course, the minister is now taking credit for the fact that it has gone down, but the interest rate is still at 13.75 per cent, more than two percentage points higher than what it was when the Conservatives were in power.
The government has done nothing to lower interest rates or cut taxes. There have been no tax cuts at all. The only consolation is that it has not levied the 18-cent excise tax per gallon of gasoline proposed by the Conservative government. There have been no measures to stimulate the growth of the Canadian economy. It is obvious, particularly since the United States is moving rapidly into a major recession, that we are going to have much more unemployment in this country in 1980 than we had in 1979.
1 would like to spend a few moments putting on the record some of the comments which were made by members of the Liberal party while in opposition and who are now members of the cabinet in the present government. The present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) said on December 12, 1979, the day before the Conservative government was defeated, as reported at page 2299 in Hansard:
What we should have had from the Conservatives last night was a budget that would reduce inflation, strengthen the economy and create more jobs for Canadians-
Where is the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce now when we need him? Why is he not saying the same things and giving the same message to his colleague the Minister of Finance? Now the Liberal government is refusing to bring in a budget, just as the Conservatives did for so many months, and we are to give the government authority to borrow $12 billion.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce was not the only Liberal member who took that line. The following day, December 13, 1979, the present Secretary of State (Mr. Fox) concluded his attack on the Conservative government with the following paragraph which is reported in Hansard of that date at page 2349:
So there, Mr. Speaker, after six months in power, this is the only record of the Progressive Conservative government: the highest interest rates that members in this House have ever seen and an unemployment rate-as the result of measures put forward by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) who does not seem
May 28, 1980

pleased that we already have such an unemployment rate-that will make it impossible for 850,000 Canadians to find a job. In addition to that figure, the policies of the minister unavoidably lead to the unemployment of 986,000 Canadians in 1980. I will end on those comments, Mr. Speaker. Such is the record of the government. It is time that we put an end to it and that we close the books.
Now, in 1980, we have higher interest rates than what the present Secretary of State was talking about last December. We have more unemployment and we have higher inflation. So much for Liberal promises.
One of the things about which the Liberal party spoke so fervently while in opposition and during the election campaign was the failure of the Conservative government to adopt an industrial strategy, a failure which led to an increasing decline in our manufacturing industry which is the backbone of every industrialized country. It seems to me that government members have forgotten the criticism which they levelled at the Conservatives and what they voted for then, now that they are in government. The Prime Minister in a number of his speeches during the election campaign mentioned this kind of need. I would like to quote from a speech which he made on February 12, 1980, in Toronto. He said, among other things, that a Liberal government:
-will convert the Canada Development Corporation into a bigger player in industrial development along the lines of Petro-Canada's role in energy.
Have we heard a word about that promise? Silence. He further said that the Liberal government:
-will capitalize on Canada's energy base in order to build a world-competitive industrial sector.
Have we heard a word about that? Silence. And further he said the Liberal government:
-will strengthen Canadian industry's research and technological capacity by encouraging development of Canadian-controlled high technology firms and ensuring that foreign multinationals expand R and D efforts in Canada.
Those are just a few illustrations of what the Prime Minister was talking about at that time. Have we heard anything about any of those promises? Of course we have not, because the Liberals are now in office and they have a few years before they must think up a few more promises. What we see is that the Liberal government is retreating from its pre-election promises of more intervention into the economy, in the same way that the Conservatives broke their promises.
The problems are becoming more serious as time progresses. In a recent issue of The Globe and Mail, Geoffrey Stevens dealt with the whole question of the need for the Government of Canada to change its ways and become involved, as other governments have in the industrialized world, in the whole process of research and development. He quoted the following paragraph from the Speech from the Throne:
My government reaffirms its commitment to increase Canada's over-all expenditures on research and development to 1.5 per cent of the value of the gross national product.
That paragraph was in the Speech from the Throne on April 14 this year. The government has been making that promise for more than a year, Mr. Speaker, and every few months putting back the date when it expects to achieve that 1.5 per
Borrowing Authority Act
cent of gross national product expenditure on scientific research and development.
Mr. Stevens went on to give some of the figures that show the real record of how we have failed. He wrote:
We haven't even tried to keep up with our industrial competitors. In 1968, Canada's 'gross expenditure on research and development' (known to its intimates as GERD) was 1.26 per cent of gross national product. In 1969, the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) recommended that Canada's GERD should be raised to between 2.1 and 2.4 per cent of GNP. In 1972, the Senate Special Committee on Science Policy (the Lamontagne committee) recommended a GERD of 2.5 per cent by 1980. But by
1978,	our investment in R and D, had, yes, fallen-a GERD of 0.94 per cent of GNP.
We invest less than half as much of our national wealth in R and D as other developed countries do.
This is the record of this government which has talked so much about the need to get our economy moving and the need to get our country moving in the direction in which other countries have long since moved.
I had the opportunity last fall to spend a day and a half in Japan. Those of us who were there were briefed by the Canadian ambassador in Tokyo on how the government of Japan, a free enterprise government, goes about promoting private industrial research and development. We were given a document prepared for the Canadian ambassador in July,
1979.	Any resemblance between the way in which the Japanese government encourages research and development in their country and the way it is done in our free enterprise system is purely coincidental.
I should like to put on record a summary of the system followed in Japan. The report to which I refer is restricted to research and development activities in the physical sciences and reads in part as follows:
The most important ministry in industrial R and D is the Ministry of International Trade and Industry, which has two R and D related external agencies. One is the Agency of Industrial Science and Technology. (AIST). The other is the Small and Medium Enterprise Agency (SMEA).
The responsibilities of the AIST include research and development of industrial technology of national importance which is conducted in 17 research laboratories, the promotion of research and development by the private sector, and the standardization of the industrial technology.
For small and medium-size companies, special care is needed. The restrictions on government subsidies and loans for large companies may be too severe for small businesses. Hence, SMEA is used for this sector.
The Science and Technology Agency (STA) in the Prime Minister's office co-ordinates and promotes science and technology R and D in five major fields; (1) nuclear technology (J space development (3) marine technology (4) disaster prevention technology (5) others, jet engine development and remote sensing R and D. Most of these areas, except nuclear technology is not yet profitable; however it is necessary for the future and hence the government assumes responsibility here.
Compare that with our government disinterest in and rejection of any responsibility to give any real leadership in the field of research and development. The report continues:
Approximately 50 per cent of the Science and Technology R and D in 1977 went to universities. It should be also noted that in university research expenditure, 56.4 per cent went to basic research, 38.2 per cent went to applied research, . 5.3 per cent went to development research in 1976.

May 28, 1980
Borrowing Authority Act
The government R and D involvement is roughly divided into two categories. One is for R and D in which the government is directly involved and the other one is where there is no direct government involvement. The result of the R and D belongs to the government in the case of direct government involvement and to the company in the case of indirect government involvement.
I could go on, Mr. Speaker. The Japanese are spending more than twice as much of their gross national product on research and development as Canada. Is it any wonder that their economy is booming, that their manufacturing industries are alive and growing while ours are declining and, in many cases, dying?
Just one last point on the Japanese situation. In their system, tax deductions are far less attractive than the other loans and tax-free subsidies which can be obtained by doing what the government wants done. Thus many corporations are attracted to the activities the government wants done.
These conditions affecting the success of corporations in getting subsidies are detailed. They include technical competence, sound planning and management, financial stability, and they cannot be a foreign-owned or controlled corporation. The cost of purchasing or manufacturing tools, machinery and buildings is also taken into account. Compare that with what we do and do not do in Canada and you will see why they are moving ahead while we are in a declining situation.
The government may want to encourage manufacturers to invest more money to improve their productivity and to employ more people. There is very little indication that this is the case.
Under the headline "Canadians Must Triple Manufacturing Spending", there appears the following article in the Montreal Gazette of May 26:
Manufacturers have to make up for lost time and invest three times more in this decade than in the 1970s, says J. Edward (Ted) Newall, who takes over today as president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association (CMA) at its Ottawa convention.
"In the 1980s we will have to invest a lot more than the $50 billion of new money that went into manufacturing in the 1970s."
Later in the article Mr. Newall is quoted as saying:
"We're looking at investing $150 billion to $200 billion in Canadian manufacturing in the 1980s. We will have to have confidence to invest that kind of money and take those kinds of risks-"
I do not know how they can have that kind of confidence given the failure of this government over the years. This government has been in office, except for those few short months when we had a Conservative abberation, for more than 20 years.
We have had a great deal of talk about the need for an industrial strategy and the need to do something about our lagging productivity, yet we have done very little about it. In an article in the Financial Times of May 26, 1980, Don McGillivray wrote:
During the past seven or eight years, Canada has steadily lost ground in some of its areas of previous economic strength, becoming more dependent than ever on imported capital and on the markets for its primary products.
Since the last recession began in 1974, for example, Canada has created about 1.8 million jobs. But only 130,000 of the jobs have been in manufacturing, which has thus declined in the proportion of the nation's work force employed.
B. W. Wilkinson, an Alberta economist, said in a study published last week that this is not so much because the performance of the manufacturing sector has declined as because it has failed to keep up with performance elsewhere. What was good enough in earlier years is no longer good enough.
His argument was echoed by the president of the C. D. Howe Institute, Carl Beigie, who said in a speech in Montreal a few days ago that incentive programs by government should favour reinvestment of profits and discourage increased dividends or the use of capital for mergers and the acquisition of other companies. Today is not the time to go into it in detail, but what we have seen in the last couple of years is a host of mergers, of purchases of one corporation by another which may have brought benefits to the corporations and their shareholders when they purchased another company, but really did nothing for Canadians in terms of improving our productivity or bringing more modern methods of production to this country.
During the campaign before the February 18 election, the Liberal party advocated a strategy which would involve more government action. Where is that government action? We have not seen it. What we need very badly is an industrial strategy which will put the people of this country to work, the more than one million people who want to work and who simply have been unable to find jobs.
If we are going to accomplish that objective and put the people of Canada back to work and find jobs for the very large number of well-educated, highly-trained, skilled young people who are looking for work now in the hundreds of thousands, work which is not there, we must have a plan. We must have an industrial strategy. We must plan by studying our economy, sector by sector, as advisory groups representing both labour and management have already recommended to this government. There should be a permanent secretariat serving those advisory committees so that solutions to our industrial weaknesses can be worked out through long-term discussions rather than enforced by arbitrary and by seat-of-the-pants decisions made because we are facing a crisis in a particular sector of our economy.
Second, we must set up an investment fund system such as they have in Sweden whereby companies are not given tax concessions automatically, as they are in our system. They are given assistance only if they place a portion of their profits in a special government organized fund from which they can receive tax benefits. This could be done here if and when they propose to expand their facilities and if and when they propose to increase their labour force in Canada.
What we do not need is the kind of thing which International Nickel did. It used the profits that it made in Canada elsewhere. It used the money, the deferred taxes, which it did not have to pay to the Government of Canada, and loans which it got from the Government of Canada, to open facilities in countries such as Indonesia and Nicaragua to mine nickel which will be sold in competition with nickel mined in Canada. This will probably increase the profits of International Nickel, but it means three or four thousand less workers are employed
May 28, 1980

in Canada. That is the kind of tax system that we have had up until now. This is something which we in the New Democratic Party want to see disappear.
We need to have an industrial strategy. We need to aim to strengthen certain of the basic industries which are found in every well-managed, successfully functioning industrial society, many of which industries are now located outside of Canada. These are industries which supply input to other industries producing final products. These basic industries include those that produce industrial machinery, industrial equipment, chemicals, plastic materials, telecommunications and basic metal fabricating products. These are the foundations of a modern industrial economy.
To meet our needs in these categories we depend very heavily on imports. When our economy is moving ahead, when it is stimulated, which is not happening now, it is in precisely these fields that we have to expand our imports. What we do is produce jobs in other countries instead of in Canada. If we are to find jobs for our people, we must substitute Canadian production to replace the present policy of importing these products. In some of these industries we should encourage such specialization and efficiency so that we will be able not only to meet Canadian requirements but to compete for a share of business on a worldwide scale.
I have used this illustration before, but we are frequently told by representatives of Liberal governments and by some of our manufacturers that it is very difficult, if not impossible, to compete with large countries such as the United States and Japan.
I have pointed out before and I will do so again that the sound system in this chamber was produced in Austria, which I suppose has one quarter the population of Canada. Austria produced the sound system, these speakers and microphones, and sold it, 1 presume in competition with Canadian manufacturers, and installed it here in Canada. I say that if Austria can have an industrial strategy and if Sweden can, both countries being much smaller than Canada, then Canada can have one too.
Let me give some examples of specific industrial opportunities that we ought to be exploring. First, I think of the transportation industry. Because of the shortage of oil and the shocking increase in the cost of oil, we must move, as other countries must move, to the modernization of our mass transit system. If we do that and increase the number of people who use public transit, we must concentrate on a new and improved technology for those systems. We can do that in Canada if we set our minds to it, rather than importing that kind of a system from other countries, something which we have done so frequently in the past.
Our passenger and freight movement by the railway must be made more efficient. Rail lines, railways, railway engines and rolling stock must be upgraded. We should be looking at the electrification of our railways. We have some companies in Canada, 1 think in Quebec and Ontario-for example, the Bombardier company-which have gone into these fields. What these companies are doing mainly are producing for
Borrowing Authority Act
sales in other countries, not for sales in Canada. That seems to me to be part of the continued shortsightedness and lack of vision governments have had in recent years.
Now I come to the automobile industry and the automobile parts industry. It has been estimated that somewhere between one in ten and one in six people in Ontario, our largest province, work in the automobile industry or a related industry. We have a deficit of about $2 billion a year in our automobile and parts trade with the United States. We must renegotiate the automobile pact with the United States with the objective of eliminating that $2 billion a year deficit. We need a greater share of the parts manufacturing industry in Canada and a substantial increase in the design and development facilities of the automobile industry. We have been restricted and relegated mainly to assembly type jobs in this country. That simply is not good enough.
Then we have the whole field of agricultural machinery. This country which produces such tremendous amounts of the world's foodstuffs is at the same time one of the largest importers in the world of agricultural machinery. The tariffs on farm machinery between Canada and the United States have been removed. We produce between 7 and 8 per cent of the North American market for agricultural machinery, but Canadian farmers purchase 12 per cent of the farm machinery produced in North America. If we produced a fair share of the North American market, employment would be increased by 50 per cent. That would automatically stimulate other industries, such as the steel, rubber and electrical equipment industries.
One last illustration is the machine industry and the equipment industry. These are high technology industries characterized by favourable working terms, high wages, high skills, clean working conditions and so on. It has been estimated that the industry now employs about 120,000 people and production is about $5 billion a year. However, we import $5.5 billion a year of this kind of equipment. We see that a high degree of dependence on imports of machinery is evident in almost every category-forestry equipment, construction equipment, machine tools and even oil and gas drilling machinery.
Even though there is a tremendous spurt in the search for oil and gas in Canada, we import most of that equipment from the United States. We need an industrial strategy. The government should begin putting into place some of the promises with respect to an industrial strategy made before and during the last election campaign.
1 want to deal with another aspect where the government has failed completely, and that is in the field of manpower training. On April 1, as reported in the Winnipeg Tribune, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) announced that a high level group of civil servants was working out a new multimillion dollar job-creation package to be ready in time for the April 14 opening of Parliament. We are some six weeks past that date-

It will be based on previous studies which have been done. We have had study upon study, task force upon task force, report upon report. In the fall of 1979 there was the review of unemployment insurance made by Mr. McCrossan. Then there was the interdepartmental evaluation of the Canada manpower retraining program. Who knows how many other departmental studies of manpower programs have taken place or are taking place at the present time.
In the meantime, the government is ignoring the critical employment problems in Canada. For example, there is a critical skilled labour shortage in Canada. In the Financial Post of May 10, several weeks ago, it was reported that:
-85 per cent of companies in the machinery industry still report at least some difficulty obtaining journeyman workers, but there is now hope that training programs now being implemented will start to meet that need.
What those training programs give us is a couple of hundred people being trained when the need runs in the thousands. I quote from another article in the Financial Post.
Thi- skilled labour shortages that have bedevilled Canada for years could be with us until 1985. That's the opinion of 1,354 Canadian companies surveyed by the Economic Council of Canada for a report to be released in June.
In my own city of Winnipeg, the Free Press of May 20 pointed out:
Like the rest of the Canadian mining industry, the north is faced with a continuing and critical lack of skilled personnel and has had to resort to importing tradesmen from other parts of Canada and overseas.
That is a quote from a speech made by the divisional personnel manager of Sherritt Gordon Mines in northern Manitoba. In The Globe and Mail of May 26 there was the following report:
Firms involved in training are mostly located in the highly populated and industrialized central region of southern Ontario, and tend to be large. These firms believe that all businesses within their respective industries should support employee training in some way.
They believe it, but they have not been willing to put their dollars where their beliefs are. They have done very little. In doing very little they have been aided and abetted by Liberal governments and many of the provincial governments, because none of our governments have really addressed themselves to the problems of manpower training to meet the need for skilled workers which we face.
We in the New Democratic Party support the principle that all firms should be involved in manpower training. This should
be based on a British type training tax whereby all companies would contribute to an industrial training fund, and whenever they trained workers they could obtain rebates to meet some of the costs which they have incurred.
Not only have we failed to meet our manpower needs to give our industries the skilled workers which they need, and not only have we continued to depend on immigration, bringing people from other countries to meet our need for skilled workers at a time when we have almost a million unemployed, but we have failed and are continuing to fail to meet the needs of the-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join in the debate on Bill C-30 introduced by the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) for borrowing authority of $12 billion for the fiscal year 1980-81, and seeking explicit authorization for the government to borrow in foreign currencies as well as Canadian dollars.
I was moved to rise to speak on this bill after taking a look at the actual bill. One of the amazing things about the bill is the size of it. It is about one-third the size of a regular page of Hansard. In that one-third page we are asked to give authorization for borrowing authority of $12 billion.
This $12 billion is to be borrowed at a time when the Liberals say they have no budget. Borrowing is taking place to fulfil the commitments made in a "non-budget" which was actually the budget the Liberals felt was so bad for Canada that they had to defeat a Conservative government. Judging by what was left out, the provisions the Liberals thought were bad for Canada included mortgage and property tax credit, energy tax credit and capital gains tax relief. It is obvious Liberals believe that putting money back in the taxpayers' hands is bad for Canada.
Then again, the non-budget ignored the question of paying for imported oil. This year, $3.1 billion will be paid as import subsidies. The Liberals say they will pay for this in a phased-out manner with a blended formula. This blended formula is a little bit to my mind like robbing Peter to pay Omar. What it is doing is taking money from Canada and sending it to the
May 28, 1980

OPEC nations in order to satisfy the Liberal's claim that they can provide a cheaper price than the Conservatives could.
There is no telling where that import subsidy will stop, no telling how long it will take for that outflow of dollars from the Canadian economy to be halted because we have improved our own production. It's a dirty trick. It's a modern-day, dirty trick on the Canadian people. It is a "robin hoodwink'', an effort by the Liberal government to absolve itself from the responsibility it has to provide for the energy future of Canada.
Recent OPEC price increases also indicate that more borrowing bills are on the way. If this is an example of how we are going to pay for that in import subsidies, government members are such profligate spenders that even at one-third of a page per $12 billion it won't be long before we have a whole book full of these bills. And that is at $36 billion a page!
Government spending under the Liberals has grown rapidly and to frightening proportions, from $12 billion in 1968 to over $50 billion in 1979. In 1978-79, the government under the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had a deficit of $12.1 billion more than the total budget of 1968. There were deficits in ten of the 11 years of his administration. I am not sure what happened in the other year.
Over the same period the consumer price index went from 4.0 to 9.1. Unemployment went from 4.5 per cent to 7.5 per cent. It is obvious that the government's policy of buying our way out of trouble does not work. Spending increased at an average annual rate of 14 per cent. As a percentage of the gross national product, federal government spending grew from 16.8 per cent in 1968 to 20.5 per cent in 1978. Spending simply grew out of control. For example, the net debt tripled between 1974 and 1979 and in 1978 alone UIC overpayments amounted to $290 million.
During the last election, the Liberals committed themselves to making no tax increases while promising to reduce the deficit in a phased and orderly manner. This is an exercise in "double-think". Those commitments are never to be kept. We are seeing now, with the proposals and the extrapolations, where that deficit will go. It will increase; it will clearly increase. Canada's gross debt amounts to $97,991 million and net debt amounts to more than $57 billion. Out of every tax dollar, 22 cents is used to pay for interest on debt which is costing us $1 million an hour. This leads to an annual cost per capita of $356 or an annual cost per taxpayer of $964. Every time this government in its past incarnations has introduced a budget within recent memory, it has spent more than it has received in taxes. These continued deficits merely add to the debt.
Mr. Speaker, there are only four ways in which the government can pull itself out of this cycle. In order to prevent deficits and begin to pay off the debt the government must do one or a combination of the following: It can liquidate assets- some people say they have already sold the farm; they can collect more taxes-and this appears likely; they can enlarge the tax base by increasing the gross national product; or they can cut back on services. The most unlikely scenario is that the government will be able to stimulate growth in the economy in
Borrowing Authority Act
such a way as to pay off our debts. It is far more likely they will follow their old pattern and actually increase government expenditures while the nation's economy sours. Given such a history of mismanagement it is no wonder the country is heading toward a recession.
The Liberals tend toward big government and bribe taxpayers with their own money. New programs are instituted and are paid for with borrowed dollars. Two years down the road, taxes are raised and then the taxpayer has to pay for the cost of the program as well as the interest on the borrowed money. Then the cycle repeats itself. The country is constantly playing catch-up to pay for yesterday's promises.
The voters who rejected the Conservative proposal that Canada should start paying her bills will be rudely awakened by the final cost of this form of government. There can be no doubt that our energy bill under this government will come as a harsh surprise. The surprise will be greatest among the members of the middle class who thought they would get off lightly by voting Liberal. Experience has shown that the wealthy have an extraordinary capacity for avoiding measures designed to redistribute income. At the same time, the poor have not benefited substantially from the government's social policies. What has really happened is that the middle class has become more heavily burdened and less able to foot the bill.
The party opposite defeated the Clark administration because it felt our tax credits did not do enough to help those who needed help the most. The fact is that our tax measures would have aided the people who would have done the most to ensure that economic growth would continue.
Let us examine some of the items which escaped Liberal notice when they decided to introduce our budget. First, a mortgage and property tax credit. This would have provided for saving in taxes of up to $1,250 on a mortgage. It would have resulted in a flat $250 saving on property tax per year.
Next, the energy tax credit. To shelter low and middle income Canadians from higher energy prices the budget offered a refundable tax credit of $80 per adult and $30 per child. Under our capital gains tax relief proposal farmers would have been able to defer from taxable income $200,000 of capital gains by transferring some of those gains to an RRSP. The common stock investment plan and changes to the rules covering RRSPs would have encouraged Canadians to invest in Canadian companies.
The differences between the Liberal and the Conservative approach include a slowdown in the housing industry, a mortgage crunch, no resolution to the real cost of energy, no assistance to farmers in fighting inflation, no growth in Canadian investment in Canada and a continued commitment to a growth in the deficit. This is the result of the Liberal plan. The Liberals have the misguided and dangerous notion that governments are more efficient than private citizens.
One of the most frightening things in the Speech from the Throne is the notion on the part of the government that the Canadian people want more government rather than less government. This is foolish. The private citizen knows when he

May 28, 1980
Borrowing Authority Act
does not have the money to pay his bills and thus stops spending. The government does not notice. The government does not understand this. Private industry, monitored by government, is, as a result of both economic and legal checks and balances, less likely to be corrupt or poorly managed than government working alone can be. However, these are facts the Grits are unwilling to accept, because if they did they would also have to admit they are responsible for the disaster that Canada's economy has become. The Liberal government is like the person who, faced with a choice between putting his money in a sound investment which would give him a return on his money or buying a luxury good which rapidly devalues, buys the luxury good. There is a heavy cost for failing to consider the future. In practical terms, this translates into the sort of government which would prefer to increase welfare payments instead of creating new jobs-unemployment insurance rather than employment insurance.
Let us look at what this sort of thinking does to Canada's most efficient industry, agriculture. Let us look at agriculture from the perspective of agribusiness. The term refers to all industries and agencies which own, manage or profit from activities directly related to agriculture. The two biggest sectors are farm supply and the food and beverage industries. The food and beverage industries are the largest source of manufacturing employment in Canada, 200,000 workers.
Farmers have annual expenditures of about $500 million in connection with their operations. They buy such things as energy, fertilizer, manufactured goods, transportation and chemical sprays. As well as the few agribusiness companies there are many companies which earn a portion of their profits from some involvement in agriculture. This includes companies like Ford Motor Company, which has a farm machinery division which is the fourth largest in the world and it specializes in farm trucks. It includes Imperial Oil, which manufactures and sells fertilizers as well as its usual items. It includes Canadian Pacific, which benefits from grain marketing through railways, owns a fertilizer plant, speculates on farm land through Marathon Realty and profits on farm fuel sales through Husky Oil.
The point of this discussion is to show that Canada cannot afford to ignore the needs of the agricultural sector. However, this government has chosen to do exactly that.
