Let us consider some of the figures on farming as they were outlined in The Toronto Sun on Sunday, May 25, 1980.
The average dairy farmer in Ontario is $80,000 in debt, on an investment of about $330,000.
The province's farmers, together, are $3.2 billion in debt. For every one per cent, rise in interest rates, an extra $32,000 in interest must be paid. And although rates are falling, the crush of the past six months has already taken its toll.
Over all. Canadian farmers owe about $ 12 billion in debt, an amount almost equal to the national deficit, and as farm
incomes decrease, that debt grows. Young farmers are being squeezed out and, as they go, so does our food supply, our lending institutions, the 200,000 people in the food and beverage industry and everyone else who depends in full or in part upon agriculture for his income. What does the government do? Nothing. It allows young farmers to go bankrupt, and by way of rewarding those who manage to hang on, when it is time for the farmer to retire, he is taxed so heavily upon the sale of his farm that he cannot enjoy the fruits of his labour.
The government says that capital gains tax relief is unfair and that there is no need to protect farmers from high interest rates and low prices. It is a matter of principle for this government-what else can it be?-because one-third of a page and $12 billion later this government has shown that it is willing to spend money. But it is unwilling to spend that money to help farmers. Capital gains tax relief is fair. It is the government that is unfair. Farmers need protection from high interest rates and low prices, but they also need protection from a spendthrift government. The national farm debt is $12 billion, and that is what is Bill C-30 amounts to. It amounts to one-third of a page and $12 billion.
How will we get those $12 billion? I can picture the solution of the Minister of Finance now. He will raise farmers' taxes. I hope the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) can justify his colleague's actions, as Canada's truly last productive industry goes under. What we do not have is a national food policy; we do not have a commitment to the farmers of the nation and we do not have an agreement between the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Agriculture. We do not have that understanding, and that is unfortunate for the farmer.
Other areas of our economy are similar. They have the same problems. We wonder now what kind of government we are getting. What kind of commitment does this government have? It originally had a commitment to a decreased deficit, and we see the results of that now. Three years of inflation will totally wipe out the commitment this government made to the social welfare of people to whom it has just given $35 by way of old age pension increases. We see an arrogance. I think arrogance can be defined as 142 seats.
Hon. members opposite are secretive. The amount of $12 billion is before us, and we have no idea of how it is to be raised or how it is to be spent. We have a government which is choking free enterprise by increasing taxes-corporate taxes are to be increased-by increasing red tape and by allowing high interest rates.
One of the worst problems is that many of the social measures which have been instituted-measures which should help people-are doomed to failure because of the lack of ability to continue to pay for them or because inflation will rob real increases.
People in the country are becoming cynical. They are becoming cynical for a reason: this Parliament is becoming irrelevant. Hon. members opposite occupy 142 seats, and now we are getting this type of bill. We are getting one-third of a page, with no understanding at all, in order to borrow $12 billion, and there is no ability to control. We are financing by
May 28, 1980

reaction and by patronage, and we are crippling our country. I think this has to change by way of responsible planning.
The first speaker to speak against this bill asked that the Minister of Finance bring before this Elouse certain measures which would allow the House to understand not only the purpose of this bill but also some of the more important aspects in terms of how the money is to be raised, how that relates to the entire financial picture of the country and what effect it would have on our economy.
It is my purpose at this time to join in asking and imploring the Minister of Finance to bring before the House all the things that the previous minister asked for. These things are important if hon. members on this side of the House are to understand what this bill is all about and what this $12 billion is going to do. 1 ask that the Minister of Finance do that.
Mir. Don Blenkarn (Mississauga South): Mr. Speaker, the bill before us is a bill to authorize the borrowing of $12 billion, $12,000 million. The way the estimates are presented to us, we have a tendency in this House to leave out zeros. Once upon a time this government said, "What's a million?" Now it says, "What's a billion?" The minister came here last night and said, "Well, I just want $12 billion". He sat down after five minutes, and that was the end of it. However, we must impress upon the government that it is asking this House to give it the right to go to the country and borrow $12,000 million.
There are 282 members of Parliament in this House. Members of Parliament are generally pretty well connected around their ridings, but I doubt if all the members of Parliament in this House collectively know 12,000 millionaires. This government is asking us in one bill to give it the right to expropriate, take, grab or borrow the money of 12,000 millionaires. I think the hon. member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin) said that this one bill uses three-quarters of a page of paper. We are asked to go along without any facts or any plan for repayment. We are asked to go along without being given any direction, any budget, any demonstration of need or any evidence other than what this overspending government proposed in what was not even a budget-hon. members opposite say the speech was not a budget on April 21. They now say they have a $14 billion deficit this year. I suppose that deficit is to be stimulative in order to get us out of the hole tomorrow. There is no plan before us. There is no budget before us. There is no policy before us which in any way indicates why we need the money, for what purpose, where the money is to come from, what plan there is for the repayment of that money or how it is going to help the economy of Canada.
We heard last night a five minute statement by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). It was his second statement in this session of Parliament. In that five-minute statement he said, "Give me another $12 billion, boys". That is not good enough for us. It is not good enough for this party, and this party will not go along with that position.
Borrowing Authority Act
We took over this government last May for a short period of time. They call it the interregnum. At that time we took over the problems which have been set out by the Auditor General. He said that they lost control of spending. We took over the problems set out by the Lambert commission and the d'Avig-non report which show the government lost their ability to manage, and they made their recommendations on how this country should be managed. We took over the disaster that was created.
They did not like us taking over, so they conspired with their friends to my left, they conned them into it and tossed us out. But the big problem is that in the interval, in those few months when we had the opportunity to look into the affairs of Canada with ministers of the Crown now sitting in opposition on this side-particularly the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) and the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cros-bie)-we had the opportunity to go over what was happening, to find out what those borrowings were all about, and how we could get out of this mess. So they can no longer come to us as they had in the past and give us the con job, because we know where the money has gone, we know where it has been wasted, and we know what to ask them when they come before committee or this House.
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) cannot get out of it with a quick little answer, as his Liberal predecessor used to be able to do; nor will the Minister of Finance be able to get out of it. It is time they came forward and gave us their plan. After all, they were all fired up to defeat the government which was elected last May. They said they had a system organized to reorganize the affairs of Canada. Presumably they had it all organized when the Conservative government was defeated last December 13. They have not produced it and it is time they did. I say to you, sir, and to the government opposite, that until they produce it, until they produce some evidence in a proper budget of how money is to be spent, a proper economic statement such as the one which was produced last fall by the former government, they can wait, wait and wait for the borrowing authority to be given them. Or they may have to use other methods.
In July of last year when the hon. member for York-Peel first took over as president of the Treasury Board, he made certain projections as to where the spending plans of the Liberal government were taking us. Those spending plans for the period from July until January, 1980, were changed and new projections made. The projections resulting from the December 11 budget represented a change in the spending program and the deficit program, and indicated control over the growth of government. May I refresh your memory, sir, by telling you that the December 11 budget presented a spending plan over four years which committed the government to no more than a growth in expenditure of 10 per cent, which was calculated to be the approximate inflation rate.
In other words, the government of which we were a part was prepared to limit the growth of federal government expense to exactly the rate of inflation and no more. Thus the 10 per cent

May 28, 1980
Borrowing Authority Act
growth in constant dollars would represent a decline in the percentage of the gross national product to cover the costs of running the federal government. The result was a definite program to reduce the required borrowings and required deficit very dramatically so that the borrowing anticipated would be reduced from a requirement of $9,940 million to $4,790 million in the four-year period. That was a dramatic reduction in the amount of money required to be borrowed.
We now have a government which says: "We do not care for those projections. We will go back to the same kind of thing we had before. We will continue to operate in the same way, no matter what the d'Avignon report said and no matter what the Lambert report said or what our Auditor General, Mr. Macdonell, said. We will go on operating in exactly the same way."
Strangely enough, the former president of the Treasury Board had a projection in his January statement of gross government expense in that period if we went back to the old plan as opposed to where we would be if we had followed the plan presented by the hon. member for St. John's West in his budget of December 11. The then president of the Treasury Board in that projection said that the gross government expense for 1981 would be $58,994 million. Actually, he was a bit low in his estimate. The Minister of Finance said it would be $60 billion, so he was out by about $1 billion. He did not think they would spend quite as much as the Minister of Finance had said they would spend. But he projected that the deficit in 1981, if the government proceeded on the same basis as the previous government, would be $14,949 million.
Let me tell the House what he thinks the expense will be next year if they carry on in the nonsensical way in which they approach things. He said that in the year 1982 the budgetary expense will be $66,354 million and the deficit will be $16 billion; in 1983 the budgetary expense will be $74 billion and the deficit will be $16.5 billion; and in 1984 the budgetary expense will be $82 billion and the deficit will be $18.25 billion. That is what they have for us, that is what we are afraid of, that is what we are upset about, and we will not support that type of program any longer.
We are demanding of this government-and we say the people of Canada will probably demand it vigorously soon- that there be some proper accounting, that there be a plan to reduce the debt, the deficit, and the amount of government expense. They have a duty to the House and the people of Canada, having taken over the government, to produce the kind of accounting that is demanded by our Auditor General and the kind of government that Lambert and d'Avignon said was absolutely necessary.
The minister says he proposes to take in taxes $45 billion and he proposes to spend $60 billion. In other words, he proposes to spend this year 25 per cent more than he takes in. For every $4 he spends, he takes in $3 in taxes. We will go in the hole by 25 per cent this year.
What has been the practice over past years? In 1978-79 we took in $35 billion and we spent $47 billion. Again we took in three-quarters of what we needed. In 1979-80 we took in $40 billion and we spent $52 billion, so the same ratio applies. You take in 75 per cent in the form of taxes to cover what you need and you borrow, beg, steal or whatever the rest. It cannot go on. I say to the parliamentary secretary, so that he will give this message to the minister, that it cannot go on. He had better come up with a plan and program to show the people of Canada where we are going.
Where are we going? You cannot come to this House and say "Give me another $12 billion", without a plan or a program. The former minister of finance, the hon. member for St. John's West, came clean with the people of Canada back in December. He produced a budget which set out what would likely be the revenue receipts and expenditures for not only the fiscal year 1980-81, but for 1982, 1983 and 1984. He set out in pretty fair detail what would likely be the unemployment problems, what would likely be the inflation problem, what would likely be the size of the national debt and where we were going. Members on all sides, particularly members from this government, stood up and said: "This is terrible, we are going to have unemployment". We sure got it. They said, "We are going to have inflation", and we have it. Let me tell you, sir, we are going to have a lot more inflation and unemployment if we carry on in the way we have been. We must have and we demand some sense of responsibility.
One of the things that bothered me, and certainly bothered the hon. member from Winnipeg who spoke earlier, was that the statement-and apparently that is what it was-on April 21 was presented to this House with a whole series of tax measures, small changes, alterations and proposals almost identical to the proposals made by the hon. member for St. John's West in his December 11 budget.
The other day I was looking for an extra copy of the statement of April 21 and I sent my secretary down to the minister's office for a copy of the mini-budget. The staff down there were very upset at the term "mini-budget". They said that it is only an economic statement. Whether it was an economic statement, a mini-budget or a Minnie Mouse budget, it certainly was no kind of accounting that could properly be described as a program on which a responsible government would come to this House looking for $12 billion.
That budget, or whatever you want to call it, of April 21 did the nickel on the booze and cigarettes, it did the nickel on corporation tax and it raised sales tax on cosmetics. Certainly the government across there does need some cosmetics. That government is trying to make pretty pictures and it raised the charge on pretty pictures, but it did nothing to come to grips with the real tax requirements in terms of oil and oil pricing. It did nothing to come to grips with how it was going to reduce expenditures and the rest of it. That is what we require from this government now.
I was fortunate enough to have the opportunity to obtain some briefing details in respect of how the financing of this
May 28, 1980

government is carried on. I should like to point out to this House what has happened with regard to debt in this country, the amount of money we Canadians owe, and what has happened over the past years.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) first became Prime Minister, or by the end of his first year, the amount of unmatured net debt of the country was $21,725 billion. By 1977-78 it had increased to $51.57 billion. At the end of October, 1979, which is the last accurate figure I have, it was $68,067 billion. 1 am told through my inquiries of the Bank of Canada and elsewhere that it is likely to be $81.5 billion to $82.5 billion by the end of this fiscal year.
This increase in debt, which I might point out was being carried when the present Prime Minister took office for somewhere around 4.5 per cent per annum and right now is costing us very close to 12 per cent to 12.5 per cent per annum, is a burden not only on us but on our children and our grandchildren. I suppose that would not bother me too much if that debt was doing something for us; in other words, if we had gone out and borrowed money like a person might borrow money to buy a home for a family, or if we had borrowed money to put in another pipeline, some more rail service or some harbours. If there were some hard things being purchased with that money being borrowed to create prosperity in the future or to create assets that would pay off the debt, much the same as a business would borrow in order to buy production machinery, that would be fine. But we have not done that. What we have done is borrow money to pay the interest.
In that alleged statement of April 21 last by the minister, he suggests to us that the interest requirement for the public debt of Canada for this current year is $10.75 billion. He wants to borrow $11.7 billion and he asks for borrowing authority to borrow $12 billion. Why he needs the extra I do not know. He says he is just borrowing to pay the bills. The truth of the matter, sir, is that he is borrowing most of the money to pay the interest. When do we get to the point where we cannot borrow enough money to even pay the interest? This is very much like a family that borrows from the bank to pay their Chargex bill and uses the Chargex or Visa card to go to the grocery store. You have to pay certain things as you go along. Surely the ordinary expenses of a country should be paid from taxes collected.
When the government comes to Parliament and says, "Look, give me $12 billion", surely to goodness they should say, "Here is why we need it, here is where it is going and here is how it will be paid back". It almost has a free lunch mentality. What bothers me particularly is the kudos which it attempted to get when it made the recent wage settlement with the members of the Post Office Department.
That particular matter was the subject of a Globe and Mail editorial this morning. I am certainly not one to read The Globe and Mail editorials into Hansard, but this editorial does say that it is a costly, free lunch. The editorial goes on to say that it is a precedent that undoubtedly will be pursued
Borrowing Authority Act
throughout the civil service and which will add hundreds of millions of dollars to taxpayers' costs.
Many hon. members will remember a settlement made by a former prime minister, Lester Pearson, when he settled with the Seaway workers in 1966. That settlement increased the wages for that one group of public servants by 30 per cent. That one settlement became the benchmark settlement right throughout the late sixties and into the seventies. What we have here, and I am not saying for one moment that the postal workers were not entitled to more money-maybe they were- is an unbudgeted-for increase in wages far beyond what the projection in the blue book indicates. This increase will require an enormous increase in either taxes or borrowing.
Yet in the budget or the material which we have before us, nowhere does it contemplate what will be required to pay that settlement and various other settlements, which will undoubtedly be required to give certain public servants who, like anyone else, need wage increases to cover inflation, the wages they need. That matter has not been budgeted for nor accounted for in the blue book or in the estimates we have before us.
When asked about this matter today, the President of the Treasury Board more or less shrugged his shoulders and suggested, "Well, that's the way it is". Apparently he was offered a wooden nickel today. The problem is that he seems to want to get $12 billion from this House. Maybe we could use some wooden nickels to pay some of the bills run up by this government. Perhaps this government had better figure out a way to make wooden nickels and to pay its bills with those wooden nickels, because until it gives us an accounting of its spending plans, it should not be coming here for a request to borrow real money.
Prior to the budget of December, this House was presented with a Government of Canada tax expenditure account book that set out all the various tax expenditures that had occurred as a result of legislation up until that time. This tax expenditure conceptual analysis was available to members of Parliament. This is the first report of its kind presented by a government which was concerned about what tax preferences were given to various people in society, how the income and commodity tax system works and what it costs to give certain benefits to certain groups in society.
That report was presented in December, 1979. The government of the day was defeated in that same month, and since that time we have heard absolutely nothing from the Minister of Finance with respect to how he proposes to treat tax expenditures. One of the greatest problems in our country is a tax system which has all sorts of little benefits, and in some cases very major benefits, for certain individuals. We have not had from this government, despite the material available to it, an analysis of whether certain tax expenditures allowed by the various taxing statutes are really doing what they were intended to do.
Once again, having had no accounting, no direction, no proposal with respect to tax expenditures, and considering that even the material analysis and work was done for it, we are entitled to something better than what this government is

May 28, 1980
Borrowing Authority Act
offering and something better than just an outright demand for $12 billion.
I would like to come for a moment to the statement made by the President of the Treasury Board when he was presenting the Main Estimates. The President of the Treasury Board said, when he tabled the Main Estimates for 1980-81 which provided for expenditures of $58.4 billion, that those estimates were prepared on the basis of economic policy and assessments of the previous government and that they were not modified to reflect the policies under development by his government. Given the time required for the technical revision of estimates, that is literally an amazing statement. We have the President of the Treasury Board, on behalf of the government, presenting estimates that he says do not reflect the spending plans of the government.
This economic statement was made in the House on April 21. On April 22 the estimates were introduced, but the estimates do not reflect the spending plans of the government. The estimates do not balance with the cash demands suggested as being required by the Minister of Finance of approximately $60.4 billion. We have a situation where this Parliament has no real indication of where this government intends to spend the money, or how it intends to change the tax structure of the country in order to collect that money. All we have today is a bill asking this House to approve further borrowing by the Government of Canada in the amount of $12 billion.
That request would not be that bad if we had figures, but we do not, so we begin to wonder why it needs all that money. In the spending estimates and proposals made by the former government, it indicated for the year 1980-81 that it would have a financial requirement, excluding foreign exchange transactions, of $8.2 billion. This government says that it may require $11.7 billion. But when one analyses the statement further, one cannot figure out what the non-budgetary transactions are because the government does not give a budget, merely an addendum.
On the addendum, it says that the non-budgetary transactions will save the government $600 million. However, the statement in December produced by the former minister of finance, and on which the present estimates are based, indicated non-budgetary savings of $1.1 billion. Again we have no idea, either in the budgetary amounts or in the borrowing requirement amounts, of where we are going.
The former government, on the basis of the Crosbie budget and on the basis of its financial requirements as indicated in the estimates, said that it could operate this country for the full fiscal year on a borrowing requirement of $8.2 billion. This minister says that he will need $11,730 billion, but he does not tell us how, where or what his spending plans are. He simply says, "Give me more money". That is not being responsible. This House would not be very responsible if it were to vote for that kind of proposition.
The budget statement-or whatever you want to call it- that was produced on April 21 by the Minister of Finance
refers to an oil policy. Buried in his speech is the following statement:
The blended approach to oil pricing, which it is the government's intention to introduce, will allow a reduction in federal oil import compensation payments from the level assumed in deriving the $60.4 billion estimate of total outlays.
That is most interesting. Later in his speech he said:
Implementing blended oil pricing could alone reduce both expenditures and financial requirements by as much as $1 billion.
That is interesting as well. Day after day in this House we have asked, "Where is the blender? How do you blend the price?" But we get no answers. We ask, "What is your oil pricing policy?" We get no answers. We ask, "Are you going to put a tax on oil at the wellhead, at the refinery, at the refinery gate or wherever?" We get no answer. We ask, "How do you blend the price? Do you go to Mexico and pay them $5 or $6 American more than any other country in the world and blend it that way? Do you blend the price by telling Canadians who want to drill for oil in Alberta that they will get less than the Mexicans? Do you tell the Syncrude-type operators that you will give them less than the Mexicans? Do you tell the people drilling off the coast of Labrador that they will get less than the Mexicans? Is that how you blend it?" We do not know the answers but we are told, "You can get a blender and it will give you a billion dollars."
This is all the more reason why we must have a budget before this bill is passed. We want to know where we are going. Why does this country really need to give this government authority to borrow without any facts or figures on why the government need the money? The estimates do not balance; the financial statement of April does not balance; we have the blender here and it does not balance. We do not even know how it is put together. Is that supposed to be reponsible government? Is that how parliament is asked to be responsible in dealing with this irresponsible government?
It would not be so bad if we were borrowing money for capital projects, if we were borrowing money to make Canada self-sufficient in petroleum or if we were borrowing money to build new harbours, seaways and that type of thing. But we have no indication what this borrowing is for. There is no indication of the reason for the borrowing. This is no way to run a government.
An hon. member brought up the question of unemployment and I want to dwell on that for a moment. The bill before us is the same old bill that we had before-the employment tax credit bill. It does nothing to improve employment; it is more of a handout, in some senses, to some employers. There is no evidence before the minister, even, that he has created new jobs with the bill. It does not help companies unless they make a profit. Indeed, our analysis shows that a company has to make in excess of $35,000 profit before it is worth employing anybody under the employment tax credit bill. That is the government's total strategy for employment. It is one of these tax allowance bills, tax expenditure bills, yet we have no analysis from the government on how this type of bill works. We have no statement in a budget to show where we are going.

This is the only employment bill before the House so we want to know where we are going before we let the government put the country, our children and our children's children further into debt.
Dealing for a moment with the way borrowing in this country operates, in his opening statement the Minister of Finance said that he had on April 1 $2.9 billion borrowing authority left. That borrowing authority is increased every time the existing debt is paid off. In other words, once you have a debt of the country you can continue to borrow up to that debt all the time. You can always borrow money to pay off existing indebtedness.
We know from reading the newspapers that there have been enormous redemptions of Canada Savings Bonds. All of the money required to pay back those Canada Savings Bonds can be borrowed again without any increase in borrowing authority. I am sure the hon. member for St. John's West expected to hear from the minister, as I did, the exact amount of borrowing authority left as of last evening -perhaps as of May 1 or May 15-but that figure apparently is not available to us.
What shocks me is the Minister of Finance coming to this House and saying that he needs the authority to borrow $12 billion when he does not know how much authority to borrow he still has. He dashed in here last night and he dashed right out again. He cannot tell us what he has still available in the way of borrowing authority. There has not been a Liberal speaker come forward to give us any indication. The Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) was here this afternoon, as was the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Evans). I have put this question now and the member for St. John's West has already asked for it. I would have thought that in the course of the debate the government would have been able to give us some figures on the borrowing authority they still have, but we still have not heard from them.

speechtext: 1 will be very brief. There is a feeling on this side of the House that the government has to do something. It has to produce a financial and economic statement before it gets approval to borrow money that is presumably required to handle all its needs until the end of the fiscal year. If it is really impossible for the government at this point to operate, we suggest that it has an obligation to advise exactly what borrowing authority it needs. We will then undertake with them, so that they will not run into the problem of being unable to pay pensions and so on, to pass temporary borrowing measures piece by piece to enable them to keep the country operating. However, we cannot see the point of allowing them the right to borrow what purports to be the amount of money-it might not be the right amount of money-they are going to need for the entire fiscal year to the end of March without some accurate accounting from them. If the government wants to get this bill through, if they want to undertake with us exactly when they can give us the financial accounting, then perhaps we can come to some agreement with respect to the amount required in the bill.
